rationale: Psalm 1 carries no superscription and unfolds as one continuous wisdom antithesis: the beatitude “Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers” (web:Ps.1.1) sets a righteous/wicked contrast that the tree-and-chaff figures of web:Ps.1.3-web:Ps.1.4 develop, and the closing line “Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish” (web:Ps.1.6) resolves; no vocative address, imperative, or speaker change interrupts the movement between the opening blessing and the closing judgment.
rejected_alternative: A closing-couplet break after web:Ps.1.4's chaff simile was considered but rejected because the antithesis continues without an address or mood shift through to web:Ps.1.6.

rationale: Psalm 2 opens without a title, narrating the nations' revolt: “Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?” (web:Ps.2.1) leads into the kings' and rulers' conspiracy (web:Ps.2.2) and closes with their own quoted resolve, “Let's break their bonds apart, and cast their cords from us” (web:Ps.2.3). The strophe is bounded by that closing quotation: web:Ps.2.4 resumes the narrator's voice describing Yahweh's reaction rather than the rebels' speech, “He who sits in the heavens will laugh.”
rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.2.4 to fold the divine reaction into the nations' plot was considered but rejected because the rebels' quoted speech closes cleanly at web:Ps.2.3 before the narrator resumes.

rationale: The strophe opens as the narrator's voice returns after the rebels' quoted threat, beginning יוֹשֵׁ֣ב (web:Ps.2.4 = oshb:Ps.2.4, byte tier), “He who sits in the heavens will laugh”, and moves through Yahweh's derision (web:Ps.2.4-web:Ps.2.5) to his own quoted decree, “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion” (web:Ps.2.6). The strophe closes on that self-referential divine declaration, distinct in voice from the king's own recitation of the decree beginning web:Ps.2.7.

rationale: The strophe opens as the king's own voice takes up Yahweh's decree, beginning אֲסַפְּרָ֗ה (web:Ps.2.7 = oshb:Ps.2.7, byte tier), “I will tell of the decree: Yahweh said to me” (web:Ps.2.7), continues through the divine adoption formula “You are my son. Today I have become your father” (web:Ps.2.7) and the promise of the nations as inheritance (web:Ps.2.8), and closes on the decree's image of shattering, “You shall dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” (web:Ps.2.9). This self-referential recitation is bounded on both sides: web:Ps.2.6 is Yahweh's own declaration in a different voice, and web:Ps.2.10 turns to direct imperative address to earthly kings.

The imperative cluster addressed to “kings” and “judges of the earth” has no antecedent in the decree strophe that precedes it (web:Ps.2.7-web:Ps.2.9), marking a clean seam at web:Ps.2.9-web:Ps.2.10.

rationale: Psalm 3's title places it after the historical note “when he fled from Absalom his son” (web:Ps.3.0 = oshb:Ps.3.1), and the eight verses that follow move as one lament-to-confidence arc addressed to Yahweh: the complaint of web:Ps.3.1-web:Ps.3.2 (“Yahweh, how my adversaries have increased!”), the confidence of web:Ps.3.3-web:Ps.3.4, the untroubled sleep of web:Ps.3.5-web:Ps.3.6, and the imperative plea and blessing of web:Ps.3.7-web:Ps.3.8 turn on repeated address to Yahweh rather than a change of addressee. Selah closes three of these verses — web:Ps.3.2 (oshb:Ps.3.3), web:Ps.3.4 (oshb:Ps.3.5), and web:Ps.3.8 (oshb:Ps.3.9) — corroborating the internal pauses without independently dividing the psalm into separate rows.
rejected_alternative: A three-part strophe split at the recurring liturgical pause closing web:Ps.3.2, web:Ps.3.4, together with web:Ps.3.8 was considered but rejected because the pause alone is not an independent seam driver and the address shifts across the eight verses are not sharp enough to carry a division on their own.

rationale: Psalm 4's title (web:Ps.4.0 = oshb:Ps.4.1) marks it lamnatseach, on stringed instruments, le-David, and its eight verses alternate address between Yahweh and the addressee named “sons of men” (web:Ps.4.2) without settling into blocks large enough to divide: the opening plea to Yahweh (web:Ps.4.1) gives way to a rebuke of “sons of men” closed by Selah (web:Ps.4.2, oshb:Ps.4.3), a declaration about “him who is godly” (web:Ps.4.3), a further imperative to the same audience closed by Selah (web:Ps.4.4, oshb:Ps.4.5), and a return to direct address to Yahweh that carries through to the close (web:Ps.4.5-web:Ps.4.8). This alternating address argues for treating the psalm as one row rather than dividing it at a particular point. The psalm also opens immediately after the Selah that closes Psalm 3 (web:Ps.3.8 = oshb:Ps.3.9), so that front-seam pause is disclosed here though it belongs to the preceding psalm.
rejected_alternative: A strophe break between the address to Yahweh and the rebuke of the sons of men was considered but rejected because both addressees recur more than once across the eight verses rather than occupying separate blocks.

rationale: Psalm 7's title (web:Ps.7.0 = oshb:Ps.7.1) is the psalm's shiggaion, le-David, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite, and the strophe moves from the opening plea for rescue, “I take refuge in you. rationale: Psalm 8's title (web:Ps.8.0 = oshb:Ps.8.1) marks it lamnatseach, on the gittith, le-David, and the nine verses form one hymn on human dignity framed by a returning refrain: the invocation “Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth” opens the psalm (web:Ps.8.1) and recurs to close it (web:Ps.8.9), bracketing the meditation on the heavens (web:Ps.8.3-web:Ps.8.4) and human dominion (web:Ps.8.5-web:Ps.8.8). The refrain's shared clause collates at byte tier against its own verse (web:Ps.8.1 = oshb:Ps.8.2) and at skeleton tier against the closing verse (web:Ps.8.9 = oshb:Ps.8.10), where cantillation differs but the consonantal wording recurs; the closing verse omits the opening verse's second clause, “You have set your glory above the heavens” (web:Ps.8.1), rather than repeating it in full.
rejected_alternative: Dividing the psalm into a frame row and a body row at the refrain boundary was considered but rejected because the returning refrain argues for treating the hymn as one bracketed composition rather than cutting it at its own frame.

The strophe ends before the following imperative summons to communal praise.

The strophe closes on the nations “sunk down in the pit that they made” (web:Ps.9.15) and the declaration “Yahweh has made himself known… The wicked is snared by the work of his own hands” — which the verse’s own Selah closes (web:Ps.9.16 = oshb:Ps.9.17), a tier-3 corroboration of the strophe’s end.

rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (tier-1 opener evidence, web:Ps.11.0 = oshb:Ps.11.1) opens one 7-verse movement: refuge declared in the psalmist’s own voice (“In Yahweh, I take refuge” web:Ps.11.1) against a quoted taunt to flee, answered by a rhetorical question about the foundations (web:Ps.11.3), then Yahweh’s heavenly examination of the righteous and the wicked (web:Ps.11.4-5), the wicked’s judgment (web:Ps.11.6), and a closing confession of Yahweh’s own righteousness (web:Ps.11.7). rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (tier-1 opener evidence, web:Ps.14.0 = oshb:Ps.14.1) opens a diagnosis of universal corruption: “The fool has said in his heart” that “There is no God” (web:Ps.14.1), Yahweh’s heavenly search finding “no one who does good, no, not one” (web:Ps.14.3), and a rhetorical charge against the “workers of iniquity” who “don’t call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4). rationale: The title “A Prayer by David.” (web:Ps.17.0 = oshb:Ps.17.1) opens with תְּפִלָּ֗ה לְדָ֫וִ֥ד, tefillah le-David, a superscription genre label (tier-1 opener class) echoed within the same MT verse by תְפִלָּתִ֑י, 'my prayer,' in “Give ear to my prayer that doesn't go out of deceitful lips” (web:Ps.17.1). Give ear...” (web:Ps.17.1) and the jussive petition “Let my sentence come out of your presence” (web:Ps.17.2) open a plea for a verdict that the psalmist grounds in sworn self-testimony through “My steps have held fast to your paths. My feet have not slipped” (web:Ps.17.5), so the appeal and its supporting testimony read as one continuous unit addressed to Yahweh, with the next vocative-imperative cluster resuming at web:Ps.17.6.

rationale: The title's historical note — “For the Chief Musician. By David the servant of Yahweh, who spoke to Yahweh the words of this song in the day that Yahweh delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul” (web:Ps.18.0) — opens with לְעֶ֥בֶד יְהוָ֗ה, 'servant of Yahweh,' and closes with וּמִיַּ֥ד שָׁאֽוּל, 'and from the hand of Saul' (oshb:Ps.18.1); at 20 MT words (sweep: 20 words) it names Chief-Musician dedication, Davidic authorship, servant status, compositional occasion, and the Saul/enemies deliverance setting that the psalm's own rescue narrative retells. The declarative epithet list “I love you, Yahweh, my strength” through “my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower” (web:Ps.18.1-Ps.18.2) states the psalmist's confidence in Yahweh before the narrative proper begins; “The cords of death surrounded me” (web:Ps.18.4) shifts to finite narrative describing the crisis, and the strophe closes on the cry being answered — “He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears” (web:Ps.18.6) — which sets up the theophany as Yahweh's response.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the epithet list (web:Ps.18.1-Ps.18.2) from the distress narrative that follows would separate a static confidence-confession from the crisis-and-cry it is answering.

rationale: “Then the earth shook and trembled” (web:Ps.18.7) opens the theophany proper as Yahweh's answer to the cry heard at web:Ps.18.6, moving through cosmic disturbance (earth, mountains), fire imagery (“Smoke went out of his nostrils. Consuming fire came out of his mouth.” web:Ps.18.8), and descent (“He bowed the heavens also, and came down.” web:Ps.18.9) to the divine mount completing the approach — “He rode on a cherub, and flew... soared on the wings of the wind” (web:Ps.18.10); the storm-cloud imagery of the next strophe (“He made darkness his hiding place,” web:Ps.18.11) begins a second theophanic movement rather than continuing this descent narrative.
