rationale: ט opens web:Ps.37.16, “Better is a little that the righteous has, than the abundance of many wicked.”; י opens web:Ps.37.18, “Yahweh knows the days of the perfect.”; web:Ps.37.17 as well as web:Ps.37.19 continue their own letter's span rather than opening new ones. Content and acrostic agree on the same four-verse boundary: a tet-yod pair contrasting the righteous few's security with the wicked's failing arms.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.37.16-Ps.37.17 and web:Ps.37.18-Ps.37.19 could stand as two separate two-verse rows, but nothing in the content marks a fresh subject or addressee at web:Ps.37.18 beyond the acrostic's own letter change, so they are kept together.

rationale: web:Ps.37.20 opens, “But the wicked shall perish.”; its surface letter כ sits at the position expected for kaf, though the word is the particle כִּ֤י (oshb:Ps.37.20, “for/but”) rather than a content word. web:Ps.37.21 opens on ל (לֹוֶ֣ה, oshb:Ps.37.21, “borrows”), positioned earlier than a strict two-verse-per-letter count would predict — the acrostic's own known irregularity in this zone. מ opens web:Ps.37.23, “A man’s steps are established by Yahweh.” The content stays on one theme throughout — the wicked's end contrasted with the righteous's borrowing-and-giving and Yahweh-established steps — corroborating the row's outer bounds even where the letter sequence itself is irregular.
rejected_alternative: A stricter reading would open a new row at web:Ps.37.21 to line up with lamed's letter position, but the wicked-versus-righteous contrast running web:Ps.37.20-Ps.37.24 is one content movement, so the letter irregularity is disclosed here rather than used to force an extra row.

rationale: נ opens web:Ps.37.25, “I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken”; ס opens web:Ps.37.27, “Depart from evil, and do good.”; the surface table then shows צ at web:Ps.37.29 and פ at web:Ps.37.30 — tsade before the letter פ, the reverse of their alphabetic order — with ayin absent between the ס and פ positions, matching the acrostic's own missing-letter table. Content runs continuously from the psalmist's life-long testimony (web:Ps.37.25-Ps.37.26) through the righteous's inheritance, speech, and law (web:Ps.37.29-Ps.37.31) to the wicked watching to kill (web:Ps.37.32).
rejected_alternative: The tsade/פ order crux at web:Ps.37.29-Ps.37.30 could be treated as two separate rows split at the reversal, but the content gives no addressee or subject change there, so the span is kept as one row with the irregularity disclosed rather than used as a seam.

device_notes: Covers the נ/ס/[ayin-absent]/פ/tsade zone, the acrostic's best-documented crux in this part; content, not letter order, drives the row boundary here.

rationale: ק opens web:Ps.37.34, “Wait for Yahweh, and keep his way”; ר opens web:Ps.37.35, “I have seen the wicked in great power”; ש opens web:Ps.37.37, “Mark the perfect man, and see the upright”; tav is absent from the span, matching its book-wide absence from the acrostic's surface table. The content closes the psalm on one continuous movement — Yahweh will not abandon the righteous (web:Ps.37.33), the call to wait and watch the wicked's end (web:Ps.37.34-Ps.37.36), and the righteous's future against the wicked's cutting-off (web:Ps.37.37-Ps.37.40) — giving the psalm's closing row one continuous content arc.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.37.37-Ps.37.40 could split off as a short shin-led coda row, but nothing in the content marks a fresh addressee or subject there beyond the acrostic's own letter change, so the span stays one row closing the psalm.

rationale: The psalm opens on direct address, “Yahweh, don’t rebuke me in your wrath, neither chasten me in your hot displeasure” (web:Ps.38.1), and that vocative launches an unbroken self-voiced complaint of bodily affliction under divine wrath — arrows, sickness, and the weight of sin — running through “I am faint and severely bruised. I have groaned by reason of the anguish of my heart” (web:Ps.38.8); the next vocative, “Lord” (web:Ps.38.9), opens a new address and closes this span.
rejected_alternative: Closing the strophe earlier, at web:Ps.38.4 where the sin-confession phrase surfaces, would split the one wrath-and-affliction complaint that runs continuously to web:Ps.38.8 under one vocative.

device_notes: Psalm 38 stands as one liturgical composition; its rows answer throughout to that one parent. Its title carries mizmor and le-David plus lehazkir (‘for a memorial,’ web:Ps.38.0 = oshb:Ps.38.1) — a label shared with exactly one other psalm book-wide, Psalm 70 (2 psalms book-wide carry lehazkir, per the genre-label inventory).

rationale: A fresh vocative, “Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you” (web:Ps.38.9), opens a unit describing failing strength, the withdrawal of friends and kinsmen (web:Ps.38.11), and enemies who ‘lay snares’ (web:Ps.38.12); the psalmist's silence before them — “I, as a deaf man, don’t hear” (web:Ps.38.13) — extends the same isolation rather than opening a new address, so the span holds to web:Ps.38.14 where the deaf/mute self-description ends.
rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.38.13-14 as its own unit is a live alternative, since ‘But I, as a deaf man’ marks a self-referential turn; it is kept with vv. 9-12 because no vocative or imperative restarts the address until web:Ps.38.15.

rationale: The vocative returns, “For I hope in you, Yahweh. You will answer, Lord my God” (web:Ps.38.15), opening a unit that moves from hope through the confession “I will declare my iniquity” (web:Ps.38.18) to a fresh description of enemies, “vigorous and many” (web:Ps.38.19), closing at web:Ps.38.20 before the imperative cluster of web:Ps.38.21 reopens direct petition.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the confession (web:Ps.38.15-18) from the enemy description (web:Ps.38.19-20) into separate rows is a live alternative, but no address or imperative marker separates them — both stay under the hope vocative opened at web:Ps.38.15.

rationale: A double imperative closes the psalm: “Don’t forsake me, Yahweh. My God, don’t be far from me” (web:Ps.38.21) and “Hurry to help me, Lord, my salvation” (web:Ps.38.22) — a two-verse plea distinct in mood (direct command, not confession or complaint) from the preceding span and closing the composition.
rejected_alternative: Folding this couplet into the preceding span (web:Ps.38.15-22) would obscure the shift from confession/complaint to bare imperative that marks the psalm's close.

rationale: The psalm opens on narrated resolve rather than address to God: I said, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue...” (web:Ps.39.1); the silence holds through “I was mute with silence” (web:Ps.39.2) until “I spoke with my tongue:” (web:Ps.39.3) supplies the colon that introduces the direct-address speech opening at web:Ps.39.4.
rejected_alternative: Extending this span through web:Ps.39.6 (the meditation itself) is a live alternative, but the narrated resolve of vv. 1-3 is grammatically distinct from the second-person address that begins at web:Ps.39.4.

device_notes: This psalm's rows share one parent unit, Psalm 39, from opening to close. rationale: The reported speech opens, “Yahweh, show me my end, what is the measure of my days” (web:Ps.39.4), and continues through the mortality meditation to “Selah” at the close of web:Ps.39.5 and on into the parallel reflection “Surely every man walks like a shadow” (web:Ps.39.6); the vocative next reopens at “Now, Lord” (web:Ps.39.7).

rationale: The psalm opens on testimony rather than petition, “I waited patiently for Yahweh. He turned to me, and heard my cry” (web:Ps.40.1), moving through the deliverance narrative to the beatitude “Blessed is the man who makes Yahweh his trust” (web:Ps.40.4) and on to “Many, Yahweh, my God, are the wonderful works” (web:Ps.40.5); the direct-speech marker at web:Ps.40.6 ('Sacrifice and offering...') opens the next unit.

observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the narrative report עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּתְרוּעָ֑ה, "God has gone up with a shout" (oshb:Ps.47.6), the psalm’s turn from address-to-nations to third-person account
the repeated imperative זַמְּר֣וּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים זַמֵּ֑רוּ, "sing praises, sing praises" (oshb:Ps.47.7), occurs four times within one verse (web:Ps.47.6)
device_notes: This strophe’s close, “God reigns over the nations. God sits on his holy throne” (web:Ps.47.8), forms the psalm’s structural climax rather than a book-boundary doxology.

rationale: The Zion hymn opens on praise, “Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain” (web:Ps.48.1), describing the city’s beauty through “Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion” (web:Ps.48.2) to the declaration “God has shown himself in her citadels as a refuge” (web:Ps.48.3), immediately before the narrative report of the kings’ assault opens the next strophe.
rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.48.1 was rejected because the description of Zion’s beauty and defense continues one descriptive movement through web:Ps.48.3 without a narrative marker like the “For, behold” that opens the next strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on גָּ֘ד֤וֹל יְהוָ֣ה וּמְהֻלָּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד, "great is Yahweh, and greatly praised" (oshb:Ps.48.2), a declarative formula distinct from the narrative report that follows

the strophe closes on אֱלֹהִ֥ים בְּאַרְמְנוֹתֶ֗יהָ נוֹדַ֥ע לְמִשְׂגָּֽב, "God has made himself known in her citadels as a refuge" (oshb:Ps.48.4), summarizing the description before the kings’ assault narrative begins
device_notes: Psalm 48 forms one liturgical unit; one parent gathers its rows. Its title carries the shir, mizmor, and bene-Qorach genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json); this opening strophe frames Zion as the city of the great King before the historical narrative that follows.

rationale: The explanatory “For, behold, the kings assembled themselves, they passed by together” (web:Ps.48.4) opens a narrative report of the kings’ failed assault, moving through their panic, “Trembling took hold of them there, pain, as of a woman in travail” (web:Ps.48.6), to the closing confirmation, “As we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of Yahweh of Armies, in the city of our God. God will establish it forever. Selah” (web:Ps.48.8), immediately before the psalm turns to meditation.
rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.48.6 (the kings’ terror) was rejected because the ships-of-Tarshish image and the closing confirmation both continue the same third-person report of the assault’s outcome without a new address.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the explanatory particle pair כִּֽי הִנֵּ֣ה הַ֭מְּלָכִים, "for behold, the kings" (oshb:Ps.48.5), marking the shift from description to narrative report

the strophe closes with Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9), paired with the confirmation formula כַּאֲשֶׁ֤ר שָׁמַ֨עְנוּ כֵּ֤ן רָאִ֗ינוּ, "as we have heard, so we have seen," echoing the hearing-motif that opens Psalm 44 at web:Ps.44.1 in a separate parent composition
device_notes: This strophe’s Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9) closes the narrative report; it corroborates the shift to meditation that opens the following strophe, though the mode change from report to direct address drives that boundary.

rationale: The meditative “We have thought about your loving kindness, God, in the middle of your temple” (web:Ps.48.9) turns the psalm from narrative report to direct second-person address, continuing “As is your name, God, so is your praise to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is full of righteousness” (web:Ps.48.10) to the closing wish, “Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments” (web:Ps.48.11), immediately before the imperative cluster that opens the final strophe.
rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.48.14 was rejected because the concrete imperative at web:Ps.48.12, “Walk about Zion, and go around her. Number its towers.”, opens a new address to the community distinct from this strophe’s direct address to God.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the meditative verb pair דִּמִּ֣ינוּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים חַסְדֶּ֑ךָ, "we have thought about your loving kindness, God" (oshb:Ps.48.10), shifting the psalm’s address from third-person report to direct second-person speech to God
the strophe’s wish, יִשְׂמַ֤ח הַר צִיּ֗וֹן, "let Mount Zion be glad" (oshb:Ps.48.12), still addresses God in the same verse even as it names Zion in the third person
device_notes: This strophe’s close pivots from wish to the imperative address that follows without a new disclosure-object marker between them; the preceding strophe’s Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9) closes the narrative report that this meditation follows.

rationale: The imperative cluster “Walk about Zion, and go around her. Number its towers.” (web:Ps.48.12) opens direct address to the community, continuing “Notice her bulwarks. Consider her palaces, that you may tell it to the next generation.” (web:Ps.48.13), and closes the psalm on confession, “For this God is our God forever and ever. He will be our guide even to death.” (web:Ps.48.14).
rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.48.14 as a coda separate from the imperative cluster was rejected because the confession “For this God is our God” answers the imperative to observe Zion’s bulwarks as its stated purpose, “tell it to the next generation”, rather than closing a distinct doxology.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the plural imperative pair סֹ֣בּוּ צִ֭יּוֹן, "walk about Zion" (oshb:Ps.48.13), addressing the community directly for the psalm’s closing movement
the psalm’s final verse, כִּ֤י זֶ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֱ֭לֹהֵינוּ עוֹלָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד, "for this God is our God forever and ever" (oshb:Ps.48.15), closes on confession rather than a baruch/amen doxology formula
device_notes: This strophe is not one of the book’s four doxology seams (41|42, 72, 89|90, 106); its unit_type stays strophe, closing Psalm 48 on direct confession instead.

rationale: Psalm 49 opens with a universal-audience summons — “Hear this, all you peoples. Listen, all you inhabitants of the world,” (web:Ps.49.1) — paired with the wisdom-instruction performative “I will incline my ear to a proverb. I will solve my riddle on the harp.” (web:Ps.49.4), where the OSHB verse pairs לְמָשָׁ֣ל (proverb) with בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר (my riddle) (oshb:Ps.49.5). This vocative-plus-genre-performative opening is the tier-1 opener signature that starts the psalm's instructional frame, distinct from the title's own genre labels “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by the sons of Korah.” (web:Ps.49.0).
rejected_alternative: Reading 1-2 alone as the opening unit and folding 3-4 into the opening meditation was considered, but the riddle/proverb performative of 49:4 belongs to the summons register, not the argument that begins at 49:5.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.49.1 pairs two imperative verbs of hearing, “Hear this, all you peoples”, addressed to “all you peoples” and “all you inhabitants of the world”
oshb:Ps.49.5 anchors the genre claim with לְמָשָׁ֣ל (proverb) and בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר (riddle) as a fixed word pair
device_notes: The strophes gather under Psalm 49 as one unit. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by the sons of Korah.” (web:Ps.49.0) carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and bene-Qorach labels; the composition is a wisdom psalm whose two meditations converge on a shared closing line at 49:12 and 49:20.

rationale: The opening meditation begins with the rhetorical question “Why should I fear in the days of evil, when iniquity at my heels surrounds me?” (web:Ps.49.5) and argues that wealth cannot buy off death — “none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.” (web:Ps.49.7), reasoning through the fact that “For he sees that wise men die; likewise the fool and the senseless perish, and leave their wealth to others.” (web:Ps.49.10) — and closes on the refrain “Their inward thought is that their houses will endure forever, and their dwelling places to all generations. They name their lands after themselves. But man, despite his riches, doesn't endure. He is like the animals that perish.” (web:Ps.49.11, web:Ps.49.12). The refrain line at 49:12 recurs at 49:20 with one verb substituted (oshb:Ps.49.13 reads בַּל יָלִ֑ין ‘does not lodge’; oshb:Ps.49.21 reads וְלֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין ‘does not understand’ — direct byte comparison across the 2-verse refrain pair, sweep: 2 verses compared), so the pair reads as a near-repeated refrain rather than a byte-identical one, and it is this recurring line, not the intervening Selahs (which fall in the next span), that closes this movement.
rejected_alternative: Splitting 5-12 at the death/wealth pivot around 49:10 was considered, but no vocative or speech-frame shift supports an internal break there — the refrain at 49:12 closes the unit.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.49.13 opens וְאָדָ֣ם בִּ֭יקָר and closes נִמְשַׁ֖ל כַּבְּהֵמ֣וֹת, with the medial verb בַּל יָלִ֑ין
oshb:Ps.49.21 repeats the same frame with the verb substituted for וְלֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין
device_notes: The refrain pair (web:Ps.49.12, web:Ps.49.20) is this psalm's structural spine, binding the two meditation panels to one parent grouping.

rationale: The second meditation restates the fate of the self-assured — “This is the destiny of those who are foolish, and of those who approve their sayings. Selah.” (web:Ps.49.13) — contrasts it with the psalmist's own hope — “But God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah.” (web:Ps.49.15) — and pivots to direct exhortation, “Don't be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased;” (web:Ps.49.16), before closing on the refrain “he shall go to the generation of his fathers. They shall never see the light. A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.” (web:Ps.49.19, web:Ps.49.20), which repeats 49:12's frame with the verb substituted (see the seam at 49:12|49:13). Selah punctuates the span twice, after 49:13 and again after 49:15 (web:Ps.49.13, web:Ps.49.15); per book policy Selah corroborates but does not itself drive the boundary, which rests on the refrain.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this panel at the Selah-marked 49:13|49:15 seams (yielding a short 13-15 unit on Sheol and a 16-20 exhortation unit) was considered as the mandated rival reading. It was set aside because Selah alone is not an independent driver in this book, and no addressee or speech-frame shift accompanies either Selah here, while the refrain at 49:12/49:20 gives the whole 13-20 stretch a matching close.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.49.13 and Ps.49.15 per the verse map (two Selah instances inside this span)
oshb:Ps.49.16 opens with אַךְ אֱלֹהִ֗ים (‘But God’), pivoting the psalmist's voice against the fate just described
device_notes: Second refrain-closed panel; both Selahs of this span (49:13, 49:15) are disclosed together per book policy.

rationale: Psalm 50's title, “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0 = oshb:Ps.50.1), sits inside MT verse 1 as an identity psalm; the verse continues directly into the theophany's opening triple divine name, אֵ֤ל אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים יְֽהוָ֗ה (El, Elohim, YHWH) (oshb:Ps.50.1). The narrated theophany — “Our God comes, and does not keep silent. A fire devours before him. It is very stormy around him.” (web:Ps.50.3) — runs in third-person narration through the embedded summons “"Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice."” (web:Ps.50.5) and closes with the narrator's own comment, “The heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge. Selah.” (web:Ps.50.6), before direct divine speech to the people begins at the next seam.
rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 50:9 to include the opening lines of God's speech was considered, but the addressee changes from third-person narration about God to first-person divine self-address beginning at 50:7, which belongs to the next span.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.1 stacks three divine names (אֵ֤ל, אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים, יְֽהוָ֗ה) before any verb of speech
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, the row's closing verse
device_notes: Psalm 50 functions as the single parent grouping. Its title “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0) carries the mizmor and le-Asaph labels, opening Book II's run of Asaph psalms; this is a divine-lawsuit psalm whose three speech frames (narration, address to the covenant people, address to the wicked) organize the rows below.

rationale: Direct divine speech to the covenant people opens with the self-identification formula “"Hear, my people, and I will speak. Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God.” (web:Ps.50.7), where OSHB stacks אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֱלֹהֶ֣יךָ אָנֹֽכִי (God, your God, I) as the speech-frame marker (oshb:Ps.50.7). This is the first of the psalm's 2 divine speeches (sweep: 2 speeches) and runs through the sacrifice polemic — “I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens.” (web:Ps.50.9) — to the positive instruction that closes it, “Offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving. Pay your vows to the Most High.” (web:Ps.50.14). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.50.6) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the frame shift, not a driver in its own right.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this speech at the anaphoric ‘mine’ sequence of 50:10-12 (the animals of the forest, the wild animals, the world) was considered, but that repetition is rhetorical elaboration within one unbroken first-person speech, not a new speech-frame or addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.7 opens with the imperative שִׁמְעָ֤ה (Hear) matching the psalm's own opening summons register
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, immediately preceding this span's start
device_notes: The psalm's earlier divine speech, addressed to ‘my people’; its close at 50:14-15 anticipates the psalm's final line (50:23).

rationale: A new speech frame opens with an explicit narrator formula, “But to the wicked God says, "What right do you have to declare my statutes, that you have taken my covenant on your lips,” (web:Ps.50.16), where OSHB marks the addressee change directly: וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים — ‘but to the wicked, God said’ (oshb:Ps.50.16). This rebuke runs through the closing appeal, “"Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you into pieces, and there be no one to deliver.” (web:Ps.50.22), and ends on “Whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies me, and prepares his way so that I will show God's salvation to him."” (web:Ps.50.23), which repeats the phrase ‘the sacrifice of thanksgiving’ from web:Ps.50.14, framing the whole psalm.
rejected_alternative: Treating 50:22-23 as a separate closing unit was considered, since ‘Now consider this’ shifts from accusation to appeal, but the same addressee and speech-frame continue across that shift, unlike the explicit dixit formula opening at 50:16.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.16 opens with the explicit speech-frame formula וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים, reintroducing direct divine speech to a new addressee
device_notes: Second divine speech, addressed to ‘the wicked’; its close echoes the sacrifice-of-thanksgiving instruction of 50:14, an inclusio internal to the psalm.

rationale: Psalm 51's title carries the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note, “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.1, web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.2), and the psalm opens with the imperative petition “Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.” (web:Ps.51.1), doubled by “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.” (web:Ps.51.2), where OSHB repeats the root of הֶ֭רֶב (wash) (oshb:Ps.51.4). The petition grounds itself in confession — “Against you, and you only, I have sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight, so you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.” (web:Ps.51.4), whose Hebrew opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮ ‘against you, you alone’ (oshb:Ps.51.6) — through the admission “Behold, I was born in iniquity. My mother conceived me in sin.” (web:Ps.51.5) and closes on the wisdom claim “Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (web:Ps.51.6), before the imperative register resumes at the next seam.
rejected_alternative: Breaking after 51:2 (petition) from 51:3-6 (confession) was considered, since the register shifts from imperative to indicative there, but both halves address God without any vocative or speech-frame change, so they are kept as one petition-grounded-in-confession movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.6 opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮, fronting the second-person object before the verb of sinning
oshb:Ps.51.4's הֶ֭רֶב (wash) anticipates the same root's reuse in the next span's opening petition (51:7)
device_notes: One composition, Psalm 51, parents this row set. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0) carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and le-David labels plus the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note; this +2 psalm's rows dual-cite both MT title verses throughout.

rationale: A cluster of renewal petitions opens “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.” (web:Ps.51.7), where OSHB's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי (‘wash me’, oshb:Ps.51.9) reuses the root already quoted at 51:2 (see the seam at 51:6|51:7), and continues through “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (web:Ps.51.10) to the climactic double imperative “Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.” (web:Ps.51.12), where OSHB pairs לֵ֣ב טָ֭הוֹר בְּרָא — ‘a clean heart create for me’ (oshb:Ps.51.12) — with a second imperative for the spirit. The span is a dense imperative cluster, the strongest of the psalm's 4 internal seams (sweep: 4 row boundaries) by imperative density.
rejected_alternative: Extending the span through 51:13 (‘Then I will teach transgressors’) was considered, since it continues the first-person address to God, but 51:13 shifts from imperative petition to a cohortative vow of future action, which belongs with the psalm's next movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.9's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי repeats the wash-root of oshb:Ps.51.4's הֶ֭רֶב
oshb:Ps.51.12 opens with the verb בְּרָא (create), the same root already voiced as a petition object at Ps.51.10
device_notes: Renewal-petition cluster; sweep: 6 imperatives across 6 verses (purify, wash, let me hear, hide, create, renew), this psalm's highest imperative concentration by that count.

rationale: The psalmist's voice turns from petition to vow, “Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Sinners will be converted to you.” (web:Ps.51.13), and moves through the plea “Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God, the God of my salvation. My tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.” (web:Ps.51.14) and “Lord, open my lips. My mouth will declare your praise.” (web:Ps.51.15) into a theological claim about sacrifice, “For you don't delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering.” (web:Ps.51.16), closing “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (web:Ps.51.17). This unit's cohortative-vow opening and its sacrifice-theology close both mark it off from the imperative cluster before it and the Zion petition after it.
rejected_alternative: Folding 51:16-17's sacrifice theology into the closing Zion petition (51:18-19) was considered, since both touch on sacrifice, but 51:16-17 argues against animal sacrifice in the first person while 51:18-19 shifts to imperative petition for the city.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.51.13 opens with a first-person cohortative (‘I will teach’), a register shift from the imperative cluster of 51:7-12
device_notes: Vow-and-sacrifice-theology unit; its claim that God is not pleased with sacrifice sets up the debated petition that follows.

rationale: The psalm closes with an imperative petition for the city, “Do well in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem.” (web:Ps.51.18), where OSHB names צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה — ‘the walls of Jerusalem’ (oshb:Ps.51.20) — and resolves in “Then you will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and in whole burnt offerings. Then they will offer bulls on your altar.” (web:Ps.51.19). The topographic naming of Zion and Jerusalem's walls, absent from the rest of the psalm, marks this as a distinct closing unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading 51:18-19 as continuous with 51:13-17 rather than a separate unit is the mandated rival: commentators disagree on whether the Zion petition is integral to the psalm or a later liturgical addition responding to Jerusalem's walls being broken, since the verse names actual city walls rather than speaking figuratively of the individual penitent. The candidate holds it as its own unit given its topographic register shift (see observed_substrate_signals), but the seam is registered as uncertain.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.20 is the sole hit (1 of 19 WEB verses; sweep: 1 verse) in the psalm for צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה (walls of Jerusalem) or Zion
device_notes: Closing Zion petition; a debated seam (see rejected_alternative) held here as its own low-confidence unit.

rationale: Psalm 52's title carries the Doeg historical note, “For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, "David has come to Ahimelech's house."” (web:Ps.52.0 = oshb:Ps.52.1, web:Ps.52.0 = oshb:Ps.52.2), and the psalm opens with direct second-person address to the wicked, “Why do you boast of mischief, mighty man? God's loving kindness endures continually.” (web:Ps.52.1), continuing “Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.” (web:Ps.52.2) and “You love evil more than good, lying rather than speaking the truth. Selah.” (web:Ps.52.3), where OSHB's אָהַ֣בְתָּ רָּ֣ע (‘you love evil’, oshb:Ps.52.5) opens the same verb the next verse repeats — “You love all devouring words, you deceitful tongue.” (web:Ps.52.4) — before the address closes on the imprecation “God will likewise destroy you forever. He will take you up, and pluck you out of your tent, and root you out of the land of the living. Selah.” (web:Ps.52.5). Selah falls twice inside this span, after 52:3 and after 52:5 (web:Ps.52.3, web:Ps.52.5); the sustained second-person address to the ‘mighty man’ is the driver, with both Selahs as interior and end corroboration.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at the earlier Selah (after 52:3) into a 1-3 and a 4-5 unit was considered, but the second-person address to the ‘mighty man’ is unbroken across both Selahs, so no independent driver supports a break there.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.52.3 and Ps.52.5, both inside this span
oshb:Ps.52.5 opens with the verb אָהַ֣בְתָּ (you love), a verb the next verse (oshb:Ps.52.6) repeats, an anaphoric repetition binding 52:3-4
device_notes: The parent relation points every row to Psalm 52. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, "David has come to Ahimelech's house."” (web:Ps.52.0) carries the maskil, lamnatseach, and le-David labels plus the Doeg historical note; this +2 psalm's rows dual-cite both MT title verses throughout.

rationale: The address shifts from second-person accusation to third-person report, “The righteous also will see it, and fear, and laugh at him, saying,” (web:Ps.52.6), where OSHB opens with וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים (‘and-they-will-see the-righteous’, oshb:Ps.52.8), and quotes their verdict, “"Behold, this is the man who didn't make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness."” (web:Ps.52.7). The psalmist's own first-person voice then closes the psalm, “But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in God's house. I trust in God's loving kindness forever and ever.” (web:Ps.52.8) and “I will give you thanks forever, because you have done it. I will hope in your name, for it is good, in the presence of your saints.” (web:Ps.52.9). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.52.5) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the addressee shift, not a driver in its own right.
rejected_alternative: Splitting 52:6-7 (the righteous' reported speech) from 52:8-9 (the psalmist's own testimony) was considered, since the grammatical subject changes, but both share the same third-person-then-first-person vantage against the wicked man of 52:1-5, and no further speech-frame marker separates them.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.52.5, immediately preceding this span's start
oshb:Ps.52.8 opens וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים, marking the addressee shift from second to third person
device_notes: Closing unit: the righteous' verdict on the wicked man, then the psalmist's contrasting self-testimony ‘like a green olive tree.’

rationale: Psalm 53 is a short, indivisible movement of six WEB verses and is chunked as one row per book policy. Its title, “For the Chief Musician. To the tune of "Mahalath." A contemplation by David.” (web:Ps.53.0 = oshb:Ps.53.1), opens directly into “The fool has said in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity. There is no one who does good.” (web:Ps.53.1), where OSHB reads אָ֘מַ֤ר נָבָ֣ל בְּ֭לִבּוֹ אֵ֣ין — ‘said [the] fool in-his-heart, there-is-no God’ (oshb:Ps.53.2) — and the poem runs one unbroken argument through the divine survey, “God looks down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there are any who understood, who seek after God.” (web:Ps.53.2), the universal verdict, “Every one of them has gone back. They have become filthy together. There is no one who does good, no, not one.” (web:Ps.53.3), and the closing hope for Israel's restoration, “Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! When God brings back his people from captivity, then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.” (web:Ps.53.6), where OSHB names יִתֵּ֣ן (Zion) and יְשֻׁע֪וֹת (Israel) (oshb:Ps.53.7).
rejected_alternative: Splitting 53:1-3 (the universal indictment) from 53:4-6 (address to the ‘workers of iniquity’ and closing hope) was considered given the six-verse length is at the edge of the book's whole-psalm threshold, but no vocative or speech-frame shift marks an internal seam, and the psalm reads as one movement.
observed_substrate_signals: skeleton sweep of this psalm's WEB span (53:1-6, MT 53:2-7) finds Elohim seven times across five of its six verses and YHWH zero times (sweep: 7 occurrences, 5 verses; oshb:Ps.53.3, oshb:Ps.53.6) — independently re-derived from the bytes, matching the book's Elohistic-Psalter inventory
device_notes: Grouped, the rows answer to Psalm 53 alone. Psalm 53 stands in a typed doublet relation with Psalm 14 (an Elohistic recension of the same composition, per the book's doublet inventory); this row addresses Psalm 53's own text and makes no byte claim about Psalm 14. The Elohim-for-YHWH substitution is this psalm's own Elohistic-Psalter texture, legitimate discussion but not a boundary driver, since the psalm is chunked whole.

rationale: Psalm 54 coheres as one liturgical composition, and this row reports to one parent. The historical-note title fixes the setting: the Ziphites' report to Saul, “Isn't David hiding himself among us?” (web:Ps.54.0 = oshb:Ps.54.1) — and the seven verses that follow run one continuous movement: an imperative plea (web:Ps.54.1), a grounding complaint closed by Selah (web:Ps.54.3), and a vow-and-report close (web:Ps.54.6-Ps.54.7), with no internal address shift strong enough at this length to warrant a split.
rejected_alternative: Splitting at the Selah (web:Ps.54.3) into a plea half and a vow half was rejected: the psalm runs seven verses, under the short-psalm threshold, and Selah is capped at tier-3 corroboration by policy, not treated as a driver alone.

a Selah closes the complaint before the vow (web:Ps.54.3)
the closing verse pairs deliverance with a report clause, “My eye has seen triumph over my enemies” (web:Ps.54.7)
device_notes: The title carries maskil, lamnatseach, and le-David labels (tier-1 opener evidence) alongside the Ziphite historical note; Book II runs Elohim-heavy here (4 Elohim / 1 YHWH this psalm), matching the Elohistic Psalter texture at this position in the book.

rationale: One parent gathers Psalm 55's rows: the composition itself. This strophe opens on direct address to God — “Listen to my prayer, God. Don't hide yourself from my supplication” (web:Ps.55.1) — and holds together as the psalmist's inner-turmoil report through the wish to flee, “Oh that I had wings like a dove! Then I would fly away, and be at rest” (web:Ps.55.6), continuing past an interior Selah into the shelter-wish of web:Ps.55.8 before the seam: the next verse turns to an imperative against the enemy's city rather than the self.
rejected_alternative: Closing the strophe at web:Ps.55.7, where the Selah sits, was rejected: the quoted wish “I would hurry to a shelter” continues the same quoted speech into web:Ps.55.8, so the Selah falls interior to the flight-wish rather than at its edge.

a Selah sits mid-quote, before the wish resumes (web:Ps.55.7)
the quoted wish runs continuously from web:Ps.55.6 through web:Ps.55.8
device_notes: Psalm 55 carries a maskil, lamnatseach, le-David title with no historical note; its rows track a plea, betrayal, confidence, and verdict movement.

rationale: The strophe opens on a fresh imperative address, “Confuse them, Lord, and confound their language, for I have seen violence and strife in the city” (web:Ps.55.9), pivots at web:Ps.55.12's “For it was not an enemy who insulted me” into naming the betrayer as “a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend” (web:Ps.55.13), and closes on an imprecation, “Let death come suddenly on them” (web:Ps.55.15).
rejected_alternative: A seam between web:Ps.55.11 and web:Ps.55.12, separating the city-violence description from the betrayer's naming, was rejected: web:Ps.55.12's “For” argues directly from the city description to the betrayer's identity within one continuous accusation.

rationale: The strophe's front seam carries the psalm's second Selah (web:Ps.55.19), closing the prior verdict before this unit resumes on a specific referent, “He raises his hands against his friends. He has violated his covenant” (web:Ps.55.20), and closes the psalm on a contrastive turn to trust, “But you, God, will bring them down into the pit of destruction...but I will trust in you” (web:Ps.55.23).
rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.55.20-Ps.55.23 as a continuation of the prior strophe, rather than its own unit, was rejected: the shift from “them” (the verdict's plural target) to “he” (a specific betrayer) reopens the friend-betrayal thread named at web:Ps.55.13.

rationale: Both rows of Psalm 56 report to one parent grouping for the psalm. This strophe opens the historical-note title's setting — “when the Philistines seized him in Gath” (web:Ps.56.0 = oshb:Ps.56.1) — into a plea, “Be merciful to me, God, for man wants to swallow me up” (web:Ps.56.1), and holds the complaint through a trust declaration, “In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (web:Ps.56.4), before the seam returns to the enemies' conspiracy (web:Ps.56.5-Ps.56.7).
rejected_alternative: Isolating web:Ps.56.4 as its own row was rejected: the trust declaration's return is split across web:Ps.56.10-Ps.56.11 later in the psalm rather than repeated whole here, so this occurrence functions as an interior turn within the strophe, not an edge.

device_notes: The title carries miktam, lamnatseach, le-David labels plus the al-yonat-elem tune name (“Silent Dove in Distant Lands”) and a historical note — distinct from the al-tashcheth tune shared by Psalms 57-59.

rationale: The strophe opens on a shift to divine record-keeping, “You count my wanderings. You put my tears into your container. Aren't they in your book?” (web:Ps.56.8), and carries the trust declaration from web:Ps.56.4 to its return, split across two verses: web:Ps.56.10, “בֵּֽ֭אלֹהִים אֲהַלֵּ֣ל דָּבָ֑ר בַּ֝יהוָ֗ה אֲהַלֵּ֥ל דָּבָֽר” (oshb:Ps.56.11), restates the trust formula's opening clause twice, with Yahweh standing parallel to Elohim, and web:Ps.56.11, “בֵּֽאלֹהִ֣ים בָּ֭טַחְתִּי לֹ֣א אִירָ֑א מַה יַּעֲשֶׂ֖ה אָדָ֣ם לִֽי” (oshb:Ps.56.12), repeats web:Ps.56.4's trust clause with one word swapped — אָדָ֣ם (oshb:Ps.56.12) “man” replacing בָשָׂ֣ר (oshb:Ps.56.5) “flesh” — before the strophe closes on a vow and thanksgiving report (web:Ps.56.12-Ps.56.13).
rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.56.10 and web:Ps.56.11 as two independent strophes was rejected: together they complete, across two verses, the same two-part trust formula stated in one verse at web:Ps.56.4, functioning as one recall unit rather than two.

rationale: Psalm 57's two rows share one parent: the composition itself. Let your glory be above all the earth!”

rationale: The parent for both of Psalm 58's rows is the composition itself. This strophe opens on a rhetorical question addressed to a debated vocative — WEB renders it “silent ones”, “Do you indeed speak righteousness, silent ones?” (web:Ps.58.1), underneath which the Hebrew term אֵ֣לֶם (oshb:Ps.58.2) is read here as a lexical crux rather than resolved to one sense — moves through the wicked's nature from birth (web:Ps.58.3-Ps.58.5), and closes the seam on a shift to imperative petition, “Break their teeth, God, in their mouth” (web:Ps.58.6).
rejected_alternative: Resolving the opening vocative to one settled reading (e.g. an address to divine or human judges) was rejected: the term stays a live crux at this tier, and the strophe boundary rests instead on the imperative shift at web:Ps.58.6, an independent driver.

Most certainly there is a God who judges the earth” (web:Ps.58.11).

rationale: One parent grouping, Psalm 59, organizes this composition's four rows. Selah” (web:Ps.59.5).

rationale: The title carries two counted MT verses — the tune note naming “The Lily of the Covenant” plus Joab’s Aram-Naharaim/Aram-Zobah/Valley-of-Salt historical note (web:Ps.60.0 = oshb:Ps.60.3, web:Ps.60.0 = oshb:Ps.60.4) — tier-1 opener evidence for the lament that follows. From “God, you have rejected us” (web:Ps.60.1) through “You have given a banner to those who fear you” (web:Ps.60.4) the strophe opens its clauses on a run of second-person perfect accusation verbs: (oshb:Ps.60.3) אֱ֭לֹהִים זְנַחְתָּ֣נוּ, (oshb:Ps.60.4) הִרְעַ֣שְׁתָּה אֶ֣רֶץ, (oshb:Ps.60.5) הִרְאִ֣יתָה עַמְּךָ֣, (oshb:Ps.60.6) נָ֘תַ֤תָּה לִּירֵאֶ֣יךָ. Selah closes web:Ps.60.4 (oshb:Ps.60.6), but the unit runs one verse further: (oshb:Ps.60.7) לְ֭מַעַן יֵחָלְצ֣וּן is a למען purpose clause completing the banner-display of web:Ps.60.4 rather than opening independent material, so the petition’s imperative arrives in web:Ps.60.5, “save with your right hand, and answer us”. A ketiv/qere note sits at the close of this span (oshb:Ps.60.7): the unpointed ketiv (oshb:Ps.60.7) ועננו beside the pointed qere (oshb:Ps.60.7) וַעֲנֵֽנִי — the kq inventory’s one entry in Ps 60.
rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at the Selah in Ps.60.4 alone was rejected, since Ps.60.5's purpose clause grammatically completes the banner-clause of Ps.60.4 rather than opening independent material.
observed_substrate_signals: Second-person perfect verb chain opens web:Ps.60.1-web:Ps.60.4, one verb per verse across 4 verses, e.g. (oshb:Ps.60.3) אֱ֭לֹהִים at the first (oshb:Ps.60.3) and (oshb:Ps.60.6) נָ֘תַ֤תָּה at the last (oshb:Ps.60.6).
Selah at web:Ps.60.4 (oshb:Ps.60.6) precedes (oshb:Ps.60.7) לְ֭מַעַן, a purpose-clause opener continuing into web:Ps.60.5, so Selah corroborates rather than drives this boundary.
Ketiv/qere at oshb:Ps.60.7: (oshb:Ps.60.7) ועננו וַעֲנֵֽנִי (1 note; kq inventory).
device_notes: Psalm 60 is the umbrella unit for its rows. Historical-note titles (Ps 60 among them) are title material, quoted like any verse via the dual-cite above, not a narrative row of their own. Ps 60 is the fourth of the book's 4 +2-title psalms (51, 52, 54, 60).

rationale: The WEB text opens a curly quotation at the start of web:Ps.60.6 and closes it at the end of web:Ps.60.8, marking an explicit speaker shift into first-person divine speech: (oshb:Ps.60.8) אֱלֹהִ֤ים דִּבֶּ֥ר בְּקָדְשׁ֗וֹ introduces “I will divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of Succoth” (web:Ps.60.6); the oracle continues “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine” (web:Ps.60.7) and closes on “I shout in triumph over Philistia” (web:Ps.60.8).
rejected_alternative: Extending the direct divine speech through Ps.60.9, as the oracle's recurrence in Psalm 108 might imply at a glance, was rejected because the WEB text's closing curly quote falls at the end of Ps.60.8, and Ps.60.9 resumes interrogative address rather than first-person divine speech.

rationale: Past the oracle’s closing quotation mark at the end of web:Ps.60.8 (oshb:Ps.60.12), this unit opens with the psalmist’s own voice resuming in a question, (oshb:Ps.60.11) מִ֣י יֹ֭בִלֵנִי “Who will bring me into the strong city?” (web:Ps.60.9), moves through the renewed complaint “Haven’t you, God, rejected us?” (web:Ps.60.10) and the petition “Give us help against the adversary” (web:Ps.60.11), and closes on communal resolve, “Through God we will do valiantly” (web:Ps.60.12), closing the psalm at its twelfth WEB verse.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this closing unit at the shift from the singular 'me' of Ps.60.9 to the communal 'us' of Ps.60.10 was rejected, since no independent tier-1 driver marks that pronoun shift as a fresh strophe boundary rather than one continuous closing movement.
observed_substrate_signals: Interrogative resumption at web:Ps.60.9 (oshb:Ps.60.11) sits outside the oracle’s WEB quotation marks.
Span covers the psalm’s last 4 verses, closing at web:Ps.60.12 (oshb:Ps.60.14), the final MT verse of Ps 60.
device_notes: This span continues the material shared with Psalm 108 noted at the seam of the preceding row; disclosed here as a typed relation, not a boundary driver.

rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.61.0 = oshb:Ps.61.2) naming the stringed-instrument setting — tier-1 opener evidence. The strophe opens on an imperative vocative, (oshb:Ps.61.2) שִׁמְעָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים “Hear my cry, God” (web:Ps.61.1), moves through the cry from “the end of the earth” (web:Ps.61.2) and the refuge image “a strong tower from the enemy” (web:Ps.61.3), and closes on “I will take refuge in the shelter of your wings” (web:Ps.61.4), the psalm’s one Selah.
rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through Ps.61.5's grounding clause was considered, since it could be read as continuing the refuge imagery, but Ps.61.5 instead turns to vow and heritage language that Ps.61.8's closing vow picks back up, so a fresh unit was kept at that seam.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative pair opens the psalm: (oshb:Ps.61.2) שִׁמְעָ֣ה.
Selah ends web:Ps.61.4 (oshb:Ps.61.5) — the psalm’s one instance, closing this span at the personal-refuge material’s end.
device_notes: This psalm's rows share one parent grouping — Psalm 61 as a whole.

rationale: Past the Selah, the unit opens on a grounding clause, (oshb:Ps.61.6) כִּֽי אַתָּ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים שָׁמַ֣עְתָּ “For you, God, have heard my vows” (web:Ps.61.5), then turns to dynastic intercession, (oshb:Ps.61.7) יָמִ֣ים עַל יְמֵי מֶ֣לֶךְ “You will prolong the king’s life” (web:Ps.61.6), “He shall be enthroned in God’s presence forever” (web:Ps.61.7), and closes with a vow of praise, “that I may fulfill my vows daily” (web:Ps.61.8), answering back to the “vows” of Ps.61.5.
rejected_alternative: Opening this unit at Ps.61.6 instead, isolating the dynastic material alone, was rejected because Ps.61.5's vow language is picked back up by the closing vow of Ps.61.8, so the two verses were kept as one bracketed movement.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.61.7) מֶ֣לֶךְ names “the king” at the head of the dynastic material.
Lexical bracket נדר (“vow”) opens the span at (oshb:Ps.61.6) לִנְדָרָ֑י and closes it at (oshb:Ps.61.9) לְֽשַׁלְּמִ֥י נְדָרַ֗י.
device_notes: Elohistic-Psalter texture (Book II, Ps 42-72): this psalm carries no Yahweh and 3 Elohim occurrences (psalm_device_inventory.json), consistent with the book's Book-II count of 32 Yahweh against 165 Elohim — corroborating discussion, not a boundary driver.

rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.62.0 = oshb:Ps.62.2), naming the Jeduthun setting (one of two Ps psalms so labeled, with Ps 39). The unit is a ring: it opens on (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה “My soul rests in God alone” (web:Ps.62.1), turns at web:Ps.62.3 to a complaint against attackers, “How long will you assault a man?”, and returns to the same confidence idiom at (oshb:Ps.62.6) אַ֣ךְ לֵ֭אלֹהִים דּ֣וֹמִּי נַפְשִׁ֑י “He alone is my rock and my salvation” (web:Ps.62.5), completing the envelope. Collated against oshb:Ps.62.6, oshb:Ps.62.2 shares no tier — real lexical substitution: (oshb:Ps.62.2) אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים against (oshb:Ps.62.6) לֵ֭אלֹהִים, and (oshb:Ps.62.2) יְשׁוּעָתִֽי against (oshb:Ps.62.6) תִּקְוָתִֽי — so the return is thematic anaphora (sweep: 6 verses open with אך in Ps 62, 34 book-wide), not a repeated line.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the ring at its individual אך-openings into separate one- or two-verse rows was rejected, since the confidence-complaint-confidence pattern needs the full envelope to complete, not one opening on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: אך opens (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ, oshb:Ps.62.3, and (oshb:Ps.62.5) אַ֤ךְ inside this row, plus 2 more later in the psalm (sweep: 6 of Ps 62’s 11 MT body verses; 34 book-wide via sweep.py --skel).

oshb:Ps.62.3 opens (oshb:Ps.62.3) אַךְ ה֣וּא צ֭וּרִי and the psalm’s later matching line (oshb:Ps.62.7, this part’s D07) opens with the same 3 words — collate.py finds the two collate at skeleton tier, with oshb:Ps.62.3 carrying a closing word oshb:Ps.62.7 lacks.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.4 (oshb:Ps.62.6), mid-ring rather than at the row’s own end — disclosed, not treated as the driver.
device_notes: This row family has Psalm 62 for its parent.

rationale: Past the ring, register shifts from first-person soul-address to public exhortation: (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ ב֤וֹ בְכָל עֵ֨ת עָ֗ם “Trust in him at all times, you people” (web:Ps.62.8), closing on the psalm’s second Selah. The unit moves through the wisdom reflection on human vanity, “men of low degree are just a breath” (web:Ps.62.9), and the warning against riches (web:Ps.62.10), closing on the revelatory formula (oshb:Ps.62.12) אַחַ֤ת דִּבֶּ֬ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים שְׁתַּֽיִם “God has spoken once; twice I have heard this” (web:Ps.62.11).
rejected_alternative: Treating Ps.62.7-62.8 as a continuation of the preceding confidence refrain rather than a fresh public-facing unit was rejected, given the shift from first-person soul-address to plural imperative address.
observed_substrate_signals: Plural imperative address (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ opens the exhortation, marking the register shift from the preceding first-person ring.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.8 (oshb:Ps.62.10) — the psalm’s later of 2 Selah instances (sweep: 2 verses); no further Selah in web:Ps.62.9-web:Ps.62.12.
device_notes: The Hebrew word for "silence" opening (oshb:Ps.62.2) דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה in the preceding row recurs, from the same root, at the opening of Ps 65 (this part’s D13) — shared vocabulary texture across the part, not a boundary signal.

rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.63.0 = oshb:Ps.63.2) naming the desert-of-Judah setting. The strophe opens on a vocative, (oshb:Ps.63.2) אֱלֹהִ֤ים אֵלִ֥י אַתָּ֗ה “God, you are my God” (web:Ps.63.1), with a נפשי (“My soul”) occurrence already in the same verse, (oshb:Ps.63.2) צָמְאָ֬ה לְךָ֨ נַפְשִׁ֗י “My soul thirsts for you”. It moves through the sanctuary vision “So I have seen you in the sanctuary” (web:Ps.63.2) and closes on the resolve to bless, “I will lift up my hands in your name” (web:Ps.63.4).
rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through Ps.63.5, where a second particle echoes Ps.63.3, was rejected because Ps.63.5 begins the psalm's sensory-satisfaction imagery that continues through Ps.63.8, not the sanctuary-vision material of Ps.63.2-63.4.
observed_substrate_signals: כן opens both oshb:Ps.63.3 (this span) and the opening verse of the next row (sweep: 2 verses in Ps 63) — a paired connective across the seam, not a driver for this row alone.
נפשי opens the part’s inclusio at (oshb:Ps.63.2) נַפְשִׁ֗י (sweep: 4 verses carry נפשי in Ps 63).
device_notes: The parent grouping for this row set is Psalm 63 whole.

rationale: The unit is bracketed by its own נפשי (“my soul”) pair: it opens (oshb:Ps.63.6) תִּשְׂבַּ֣ע נַפְשִׁ֑י “My soul shall be satisfied” (web:Ps.63.5) and closes (oshb:Ps.63.9) דָּבְקָ֣ה נַפְשִׁ֣י “My soul stays close to you” (web:Ps.63.8), moving through night-watch meditation (web:Ps.63.6) and the refuge image “the shadow of your wings” (web:Ps.63.7).
rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.63.7 instead of Ps.63.8 was rejected, since Ps.63.8's closing 'my soul' clause closes the same bracket that Ps.63.5's opening clause begins.
observed_substrate_signals: נפשי opens the span at (oshb:Ps.63.6) נַפְשִׁ֑י and closes it at (oshb:Ps.63.9) נַפְשִׁ֣י — an internal lexical inclusio.

rationale: An adversative pivot opens this unit away from the psalmist’s own voice: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה “But those who seek my soul to destroy it” (web:Ps.63.9), continuing through “They shall be jackal food” (web:Ps.63.10) to a second adversative, (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ “But the king shall rejoice in God” (web:Ps.63.11), the psalm’s closing verse.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the enemies' judgment (Ps.63.9-63.10) from the king's contrasting joy (Ps.63.11) into separate rows was rejected, since both share the adversative pivot away from the psalmist's own voice and no independent driver separates them.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה (“but they”) opens the enemies’ judgment; (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ (“but the king”) opens the closing verse — two adversative openings inside a 3-verse unit.
נפשי recurs once more at (oshb:Ps.63.10) יְבַקְשׁ֣וּ נַפְשִׁ֑י, the part’s 4th instance in Ps 63, now naming the object the enemies seek — an ironic reversal of the row at Ps.63.5-63.8.

rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.64.0 = oshb:Ps.64.2). The unit opens on imperative petition, (oshb:Ps.64.2) שְׁמַע אֱלֹהִ֣ים “Hear my voice, God, in my complaint” (web:Ps.64.1), “Hide me from the conspiracy of the wicked” (web:Ps.64.2), then continues in an אשר relative clause describing the plotters, (oshb:Ps.64.4) אֲשֶׁ֤ר “who sharpen their tongue like a sword” (web:Ps.64.3), through their secrecy (web:Ps.64.4-web:Ps.64.5) to “Surely man’s mind and heart are cunning” (web:Ps.64.6).
rejected_alternative: Isolating the opening plea (Ps.64.1-64.2) from the description of the plotters (Ps.64.3-64.6) as separate rows was rejected, since Ps.64.3's relative clause grammatically continues Ps.64.2's 'evildoers' rather than opening independent material.
observed_substrate_signals: אשר relative clause opens (oshb:Ps.64.4) אֲשֶׁ֤ר, tying the plotters’ description back to the “evildoers” of the preceding verse.
Third-person plural verbs for “they/their” run continuously from oshb:Ps.64.4 through the end of this span.
device_notes: Psalm 64 forms one parent composition; its rows answer to that one grouping.

rationale: A reversal opens this unit with God as subject in place of the plotters: (oshb:Ps.64.8) וַיֹּרֵ֗ם אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים “But God will shoot at them” (web:Ps.64.7), “Their own tongues shall ruin them” (web:Ps.64.8), “All mankind shall be afraid” (web:Ps.64.9), closing on “The righteous shall be glad in Yahweh” (web:Ps.64.10) with (oshb:Ps.64.11) בַּ֭יהוָה — this part’s one Yahweh occurrence (psalm_device_inventory.json: Ps 64 yhwh=1, elohim=3; Ps 60-65 together carry 1 yhwh against 22 elohim, Elohistic-Psalter texture).
rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.64.9 instead of Ps.64.10 was rejected, since the universal fear of Ps.64.9 and the righteous celebration of Ps.64.10 both continue the aftermath introduced by the divine reversal at Ps.64.7.
observed_substrate_signals: Subject shift to God opens (oshb:Ps.64.8) וַיֹּרֵ֗ם אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים, reversing the previous unit’s “they” subject.
(oshb:Ps.64.11) בַּ֭יהוָה (Yahweh) is this row’s and this part’s one Yahweh occurrence (device inventory count: 1).

rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.65.0 = oshb:Ps.65.2). This unit opens the Zion/temple material, (oshb:Ps.65.2) לְךָ֤ דֻֽמִיָּ֬ה תְהִלָּ֓ה אֱלֹ֘הִ֥ים בְּצִיּ֑וֹן “Praise waits for you, God, in Zion” (web:Ps.65.1), moves through “You who hear prayer” (web:Ps.65.2) and the atonement confession “you atoned for our transgressions” (web:Ps.65.3), closing on the temple-dweller beatitude “Blessed is the one whom you choose” (web:Ps.65.4).
rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through Ps.65.5 was rejected, since that verse turns to God's awesome deeds and cosmic power rather than the Zion/temple material of Ps.65.1-65.4.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.65.2) לְךָ֤ דֻֽמִיָּ֬ה (“silence to-you”, i.e. “praise waits”) opens the psalm, from the same root quoted twice in Ps 62 (this part’s D06) — shared vocabulary, not a boundary signal.
device_notes: Psalm 65 is one parent composition spanning its own rows.

rationale: Register turns from temple-address to cosmic praise: (oshb:Ps.65.6) נ֤וֹרָא֨וֹת בְּצֶ֣דֶק “By awesome deeds of righteousness, you answer us” (web:Ps.65.5), then a run of participial predicates for God’s acts, (oshb:Ps.65.7) מֵכִ֣ין הָרִ֣ים “you form the mountains” (web:Ps.65.6) and (oshb:Ps.65.8) מַשְׁבִּ֤יחַ “You still the roaring of the seas” (web:Ps.65.7), closing on the distant peoples’ awe, “They also who dwell in faraway places are afraid at your wonders” (web:Ps.65.8).
rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.65.7 instead of Ps.65.8 was rejected, since Ps.65.8's report of the distant peoples' awe still describes the effect of the cosmic acts introduced in Ps.65.6-65.7, before the harvest material begins at Ps.65.9.
observed_substrate_signals: A mountain-forming participle opens one verse, (oshb:Ps.65.7) מֵכִ֣ין, and a sea-stilling participle opens the next in the same grammatical form, (oshb:Ps.65.8) מַשְׁבִּ֤יחַ (2 verses).

rationale: A tense/topic pivot opens the harvest hymn proper: (oshb:Ps.65.10) פָּקַ֥דְתָּ הָאָ֨רֶץ “You visit the earth, and water it” (web:Ps.65.9), moving through the furrows and showers (web:Ps.65.10-web:Ps.65.11) and the grasslands (web:Ps.65.12), closing the psalm — and the Davidic run the book strategy places from Ps 51 through Ps 65 in Book II — on personified nature: (oshb:Ps.65.14) יִ֝תְרוֹעֲע֗וּ אַף יָשִֽׁירוּ “They shout for joy! They also sing.” (web:Ps.65.13).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the closing harvest unit at the shift from divine action (Ps.65.9-65.11) to personified nature (Ps.65.12-65.13) was rejected, since no independent tier-1 driver marks that shift as a fresh strophe rather than the harvest hymn's closing crescendo.
observed_substrate_signals: Perfect-tense 2ms verb for God’s action opens the unit, (oshb:Ps.65.10) פָּקַ֥דְתָּ, before the closing verse turns to 3rd-person nature imagery at (oshb:Ps.65.14) לָבְשׁ֬וּ.

rationale: Psalm 66 opens on a two-line imperative summons, “Make a joyful shout to God, all the earth!” (web:Ps.66.1), continuing “Sing to the glory of his name! Offer glory and praise!” (web:Ps.66.2); the address then turns to quoted second-person speech to God through web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4, closing on the nations' submission and a Selah (web:Ps.66.4). The imperative opening plus the Selah close bound this strophe.
rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.66.7 to gather both Selah-closed calls into one span was rejected: web:Ps.66.5 reopens with its own imperative, “Come, and see” (web:Ps.66.5), a fresh address distinct from the quoted speech of web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative doublet “Make a joyful shout” / “Sing to the glory of his name” opens the summons (web:Ps.66.1-web:Ps.66.2).
The address to God shifts into quoted second-person speech through web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4.
A Selah closes the strophe at web:Ps.66.4.
device_notes: The whole-psalm parent for these rows is Psalm 66. The title carries mizmor, shir, and lamnatseach labels (tier-1 opener evidence) with no historical note or Davidic ascription; MT holds the title as the prefix of 66:1 rather than a counted verse (web:Ps.66.0 = oshb:Ps.66.1).

rationale: A fresh imperative reopens the address, “Come, and see God’s deeds— awesome work on behalf of the children of men.” (web:Ps.66.5), recalling the exodus in miniature, “He turned the sea into dry land.” (web:Ps.66.6), and closing on divine kingship, “He rules by his might forever.” (web:Ps.66.7). A Selah already closed the preceding summons at web:Ps.66.4; a second Selah closes this recollection at web:Ps.66.7, bracketing the two calls to worship that open the psalm.
rejected_alternative: Closing this strophe at web:Ps.66.6, before the kingship declaration, was rejected: web:Ps.66.7's declaration of divine rule continues the same recollection through to its own Selah rather than opening a new address.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Come, and see” reopens the strophe after the Selah at web:Ps.66.4 (web:Ps.66.5).
Selah closes web:Ps.66.4 (front seam of this strophe) and again web:Ps.66.7 (this strophe's own close).
MT Ps.66.7 (web:Ps.66.7) carries a ketiv/qere note in the inventory, not engaged by the English-level warrant argued here.

rationale: A second imperative redirects the address to “you peoples” — “Praise our God, you peoples! Make the sound of his praise heard,” (web:Ps.66.8) — opening a national testing report that runs “For you, God, have tested us. You have refined us, as silver is refined.” (web:Ps.66.10) through captivity, fire, and water to “the place of abundance” (web:Ps.66.12). The plural first-person voice (us, our) running through web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12 stops at this strophe's close; web:Ps.66.13 turns to a singular first-person vow, the seam this row's boundary answers to.
rejected_alternative: Closing this strophe at web:Ps.66.9 and reopening at web:Ps.66.10 was rejected: no imperative, vocative, or addressee shift separates the “preserves our life” clause of web:Ps.66.9 from the testing report that follows it.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Praise our God, you peoples!” reopens the address after web:Ps.66.7's Selah (web:Ps.66.8).
Plural pronouns (us, our) run through web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12: “tested us”, “You have refined us,” “our backs” (web:Ps.66.8, web:Ps.66.10-web:Ps.66.11).
The report moves from testing and refining (web:Ps.66.10) through captivity (web:Ps.66.11) to “the place of abundance” (web:Ps.66.12), this strophe's own close.

rationale: The pronoun shifts from plural to singular first person at this row's opening, “I will come into your temple with burnt offerings. I will pay my vows to you,” (web:Ps.66.13), continuing the individual vow through “which my lips promised, and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress.” (web:Ps.66.14) to a closing sacrificial description, “I will offer to you burnt offerings of fat animals, with the offering of rams, I will offer bulls with goats.” (web:Ps.66.15), marked by a Selah. The we-to-I pronoun turn at web:Ps.66.12-web:Ps.66.13 is the psalm's internal seam: the testing report speaks for a community (“us,” “our”) through web:Ps.66.12, and this row opens on an individual vow (“I,” “my”) that runs uninterrupted to this strophe's own close.
rejected_alternative: Opening this row at web:Ps.66.12 rather than web:Ps.66.13 was rejected: web:Ps.66.12's pronoun set (us, our) belongs to the preceding community report; web:Ps.66.13 is where the vow's singular first-person voice begins.
observed_substrate_signals: The pronoun set turns from plural (us, our; web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12) to singular (I, my; web:Ps.66.13-web:Ps.66.15) exactly at this row's opening.
The vow register (“I will come”, “I will pay”, “I will offer”) runs web:Ps.66.13-web:Ps.66.15.
A Selah closes the vow at web:Ps.66.15.

rationale: A fresh imperative reopens the address to a human audience, “Come and hear, all you who fear God. I will declare what he has done for my soul.” (web:Ps.66.16), continuing the individual testimony through “If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn’t have listened.” (web:Ps.66.18) to a closing benediction, “Blessed be God, who has not turned away my prayer, nor his loving kindness from me.” (web:Ps.66.20). The imperative “Come and hear” addressed to “you who fear God” reopens the vocative register carried earlier by web:Ps.66.5's “Come, and see”, marking a fresh unit after the vow's Selah close at web:Ps.66.15.
rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.66.16-web:Ps.66.20 into the preceding vow strophe was rejected: the vow's Selah at web:Ps.66.15 closes the sacrificial description, and web:Ps.66.16 opens a new imperative addressed outward to “all you who fear God” rather than continuing the vow's own first-person report to God.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Come and hear” reopens direct address to a human audience after the Selah at web:Ps.66.15 (web:Ps.66.16).

Psalm 40 closes its parallel clause ‘יִגְדַּ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה’ (oshb:Ps.40.17), ‘let Yahweh be exalted’ (web:Ps.40.16); Psalm 70's own closing clause reads ‘יִגְדַּ֣ל אֱלֹהִ֑ים’ (oshb:Ps.70.5), ‘let God be exalted’ (web:Ps.70.4) — a one-word divine-name substitution in an otherwise matching clause. This Elohim/Yahweh texture is this row's own legitimate discussion, not a boundary driver, since the psalm is chunked whole; it addresses Psalm 70's own text and makes no claim about which composition is prior.

rationale: Psalm 71 carries no title — WEB renders no unnumbered title line for it, and its numbering is identity (WEB verse = MT verse) — so the opening row begins directly at web:Ps.71.1, “In you, Yahweh, I take refuge. Never let me be disappointed.” The imperative cluster that follows — “Deliver me…rescue me…Turn your ear to me, and save me” (web:Ps.71.2) — closes with ‘כִּֽי סַלְעִ֖י וּמְצוּדָתִ֣י אָֽתָּה’ (oshb:Ps.71.3), “for you are my rock and my fortress” (web:Ps.71.3). web:Ps.71.5 shifts to a youth-and-birth retrospective register, closing this opening refuge-and-rescue cluster at web:Ps.71.4's plea to be rescued “from the hand of the wicked”.
rejected_alternative: Extending this row through web:Ps.71.8's praise vow was weighed and set aside: web:Ps.71.5 opens a distinct retrospective register (“my confidence from my youth”) rather than continuing the imperative petitions.

rationale: The span opens on a causal retrospective, “For you are my hope, Lord Yahweh, my confidence from my youth” (web:Ps.71.5), and continues “I have relied on you from the womb…I will always praise you” (web:Ps.71.6) — birth-trust language that parallels Psalm 22's own “you brought me out of the womb…I was thrown on you from my mother's womb” (web:Ps.22.9-web:Ps.22.10), a Psalter-internal parallel decided from this psalm's own text, not a boundary driver. The span closes “My mouth shall be filled with your praise, with your honor all day long” (web:Ps.71.8), before web:Ps.71.9 opens an explicit old-age plea.
rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.71.9's old-age plea into this span was considered but rejected because that verse names “old age” and “strength fails” explicitly, a vocabulary shift from the youth-and-birth retrospective of web:Ps.71.5-Ps.71.8.

rationale: The strophe opens “Don't reject me in my old age. Don't forsake me when my strength fails” (web:Ps.71.9), an explicit vocabulary shift from the youth-and-birth retrospective of web:Ps.71.5-Ps.71.8. The enemies' conspiracy follows with quoted speech, “God has forsaken him. Pursue and take him, for no one will rescue him” (web:Ps.71.11), an imperative counter-petition, “God, don't be far from me. My God, hurry to help me” (web:Ps.71.12), and closes with imprecation against the accusers (web:Ps.71.13). web:Ps.71.14 opens with an adversative pivot, closing this old-age-and-enemies span.
rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.71.11's quoted taunt was considered but rejected because the counter-petition of web:Ps.71.12 and the imprecation of web:Ps.71.13 continue addressing the same conspiracy without a new vocative or topic shift.

rationale: The strophe opens וַ֭אֲנִי, “But I will always hope, and will add to all of your praise” (web:Ps.71.14 = oshb:Ps.71.14), an adversative pivot from the imprecation of web:Ps.71.13 into a continual-praise vow. It extends through “though I don't know its full measure” (web:Ps.71.15) and the “mighty acts of the Lord Yahweh” (web:Ps.71.16), then closes on an explicit callback: “when I am old and gray-haired, God, don't forsake me, until I have declared your strength to the next generation” (web:Ps.71.18), resolving the old-age anxiety opened at web:Ps.71.9 into a generational purpose. web:Ps.71.19 opens a rhetorical “who is like you” exclamation, closing this span.

It moves into a retrospective on “many and bitter troubles” and a restoration plea, “bring us up again from the depths of the earth” (web:Ps.71.20), closing “Increase my honor and comfort me again” (web:Ps.71.21). web:Ps.71.22 opens a closing praise vow naming specific instruments, distinct from this retrospective-and-restoration span.

rationale: The li-Shlomo title sits inside MT verse 1 (web:Ps.72.0 = oshb:Ps.72.1) and opens straight into a petition: the imperative תֵּ֑ן (oshb:Ps.72.1), “give,” asks God for the king's own justice — “God, give the king your justice; your righteousness to the royal son.” (web:Ps.72.1) The verb chain then runs third-person masculine singular about the king — יִשְׁפֹּ֤ט, ‘he will judge’ (oshb:Ps.72.4) — through the close of verse 4. Verse 5 turns the subject plural (the peoples who fear him, oshb:Ps.72.5), which is where this strophe ends.
rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe through verse 11 to cover the whole royal-dominion movement was rejected because the 3ms-to-3mp subject shift at verse 5 is a concrete grammatical seam inside that stretch.

rationale: Verse 5 opens on the plural יִֽירָא֥וּךָ, ‘they shall fear you’ (oshb:Ps.72.5): “They shall fear you while the sun endures; and as long as the moon, throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.72.5) The unit continues into the dominion imagery of מִיָּ֣ם עַד יָ֑ם, ‘from sea to sea’ (oshb:Ps.72.8), and closes on the nations' homage: “Yes, all kings shall fall down before him. All nations shall serve him.” (web:Ps.72.11) Verse 12 opens a new clause on the causal כִּֽי (oshb:Ps.72.12), which marks the boundary here.
rejected_alternative: Folding verses 5-7 (the reign's perpetuity) and 8-11 (its territorial reach) into two separate rows was rejected since both share the same 3mp/3ms future-tense description of the king begun at verse 5, and the causal כי that opens verse 12 is the nearer grammatical break.

rationale: וֵ֭אלֹהִים, ‘yet God’ (oshb:Ps.74.12), pivots away from complaint into a hymnic recital: “Yet God is my King of old, working salvation throughout the earth.” (web:Ps.74.12) The recital opens each following clause on the emphatic pronoun אַתָּ֤ה, “you” (oshb:Ps.74.13, repeated through verse 17: sweep: skeleton אתה, 5 verses — 74:13-17), running through “You have set all the boundaries of the earth. You have made summer and winter.” (web:Ps.74.17) Verse 18 returns to the imperative “remember,” closing this strophe.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the creation recital (13-17) from its adversative opening (12) into two rows was rejected because verse 12's adversative opening introduces the very subject (“God”) that the emphatic “you” clauses of 13-17 continue to address.

oshb:Ps.74.18 returns to imperative petition
device_notes: The emphatic atah (“you”) opens or reinforces the clause in 5 verses of this recital (74:13-17; sweep: skeleton atah, 5 verses), the psalm's densest anaphoric run.

rationale: זְכָר, “remember” (oshb:Ps.74.18), returns to the imperative that opened the petition at verse 2, now applied to the enemy's mockery: “Remember this, that the enemy has mocked you, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.74.18) The same imperative recurs at זְכֹ֥ר (oshb:Ps.74.22), alongside קוּמָ֣ה, “arise” (oshb:Ps.74.22): “Arise, God! Plead your own cause.” (web:Ps.74.22) The psalm closes on “The tumult of those who rise up against you ascends continually.” (web:Ps.74.23) No further verse follows.
rejected_alternative: Separating verse 22's “arise” imperative into its own row was rejected because it stands inside one continuous petition with the “remember” imperatives of 18 and 22, closing the psalm as one continuous unit.

device_notes: The imperative zakhar/zekhor (“remember”) opens 3 verses of this psalm (74:2, 74:18, 74:22; sweep: skeleton zakhar, 3 verses), framing the opening petition and its return here.

rationale: Psalm 75 is a shift+1 psalm: the lamnatseach/al-tashcheth/mizmor/shir/le-Asaph title occupies MT verse 1 in full (web:Ps.75.0 = oshb:Ps.75.1), so WEB verse 1 dual-cites oshb:Ps.75.2. It opens on the first-person-plural ה֘וֹדִ֤ינוּ, ‘we give thanks’ (web:Ps.75.1 = oshb:Ps.75.2): “We give thanks to you, God. We give thanks, for your Name is near.” (web:Ps.75.1) Verse 2 switches to a first-person-singular voice (web:Ps.75.2 = oshb:Ps.75.3), which closes this strophe at the person shift.
rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the divine oracle that follows was rejected because its grammatical person (1cp “we”) differs from the 1cs “I” that opens verse 2.

oshb:Ps.75.3 shifts to 1cs grammatical person
device_notes: The rows here belong together under Psalm 75. The psalm carries the mizmor, shir, lamnatseach, le-Asaph, and al-tashcheth labels and continues the Asaph collection (73-83) inside Book III; it is a shift+1 psalm (title = MT v1), unlike the three identity psalms preceding it in this part.

rationale: Verse 2 opens a first-person divine oracle on אֲ֝נִ֗י, “I” (web:Ps.75.2 = oshb:Ps.75.3): “When I choose the appointed time, I will judge blamelessly.” (web:Ps.75.2) The same voice continues with אָנֹכִ֨י, “I” (web:Ps.75.3 = oshb:Ps.75.4): “The earth and all its inhabitants quake. I firmly hold its pillars. Selah.” (web:Ps.75.3) and is framed explicitly by the quotative אָמַ֣רְתִּי, ‘I said’ (web:Ps.75.4 = oshb:Ps.75.5), which introduces direct speech to the arrogant: “Don't boast!” (web:Ps.75.4) The quoted speech closes at verse 5's “Don't speak with a stiff neck.” (web:Ps.75.5) Verse 6 shifts to third-person reflection about God, closing this strophe at the oracle's own frame.
rejected_alternative: Reading verses 2-3 as the psalmist's own vow rather than a divine oracle was rejected because verse 4's own quotative frame (“I said to the arrogant”) retroactively marks the preceding first-person clauses as reported first-person speech addressed to the arrogant and wicked, not the congregation's own words.

rationale: Verse 6 opens on כִּ֤י לֹ֣א, ‘for not’ (web:Ps.75.6 = oshb:Ps.75.7), returning to third-person reflection about God rather than God's own first-person voice: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor yet from the south, comes exaltation.” (web:Ps.75.6) The unit closes on כִּ֤י כ֪וֹס, ‘for a cup’ (web:Ps.75.8 = oshb:Ps.75.9): “For in Yahweh's hand there is a cup ... the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.” (web:Ps.75.8) Verse 9 returns to a first-person singular vow (web:Ps.75.9 = oshb:Ps.75.10), closing this strophe.
rejected_alternative: Reading this unit as a continuation of the divine oracle was rejected because its verbs describe God in the third person (“He puts down one, and lifts up another.” web:Ps.75.7) rather than voicing God's own first-person speech as verses 2-5 do.

rationale: וַ֭אֲנִי, ‘but I’ (web:Ps.75.9 = oshb:Ps.75.10), opens the closing vow: “But I will declare this forever: I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.” (web:Ps.75.9) The psalm ends on “I will cut off all the horns of the wicked, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.” (web:Ps.75.10) No further verse follows; the strophe runs to the psalm's end.
rejected_alternative: Reading the closing vow as a continuation of the divine oracle's own voice was rejected because its fronted independent pronoun echoes the psalmist's congregational register from verse 1, not the quotative frame that bounded the oracle at verses 2-5.

rationale: The opening row carries the title's dual-cite (web:Ps.76.0 = oshb:Ps.76.1); the counted verses open in the third person, “In Judah, God is known. His name is great in Israel” (web:Ps.76.1), matching the Hebrew “נוֹדָ֣ע בִּֽיהוּדָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.76.2). The next verse locates that renown geographically: “His tabernacle is also in Salem. His dwelling place in Zion” (web:Ps.76.2; oshb:Ps.76.3 “בְשָׁלֵ֣ם סֻכּ֑וֹ וּמְע֖וֹנָת֣וֹ בְצִיּֽוֹן”). The locative opening of web:Ps.76.3 (oshb:Ps.76.4), “There he broke the flaming arrows of the bow…” (“שָׁ֭מָּה שִׁבַּ֣ר רִשְׁפֵי קָ֑שֶׁת”), ties the disarmament report back to that same site, and the unit closes on Selah (“סֶֽלָה”, oshb:Ps.76.4). A second-person address opens immediately after at web:Ps.76.4 (“Glorious are you…”), marking the boundary: the third-person report register of web:Ps.76.1-3 gives way to sustained direct address.
rejected_alternative: A seam could instead be drawn after web:Ps.76.2, isolating the renown declaration from the Zion/Salem dwelling notice, but both clauses share the same third-person report register with no address or genre shift between them, so 76:1-3 are kept together through the corroborating Selah (web:Ps.76.3 = oshb:Ps.76.4).

device_notes: Psalm 76 forms a single liturgical unit; every row here shares that one parent. The title carries four byte-swept genre labels (mizmor, shir, lamnatseach, le-Asaph) placing it among the twelve le-Asaph superscriptions of Book III.

rationale: Second-person address to God opens the row at web:Ps.76.4 (“Glorious are you, and excellent…”) immediately after the Selah closing the prior unit (web:Ps.76.3 = oshb:Ps.76.4, “סֶֽלָה”), and the same address sustains through the vocative at web:Ps.76.6, “At your rebuke, God of Jacob…” (oshb:Ps.76.7 “אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֑ב”), and the fear-vocabulary of web:Ps.76.7-8 (“You, even you, are to be feared… You pronounced judgment from heaven…”). The row closes on a return to third-person narration and the psalm's second Selah: “when God arose to judgment, to save all the afflicted ones of the earth. Selah” (web:Ps.76.9; oshb:Ps.76.10 “לְהוֹשִׁ֖יעַ כָּל עַנְוֵי אֶ֣רֶץ סֶֽלָה”).
rejected_alternative: The row could be split at 76:6/76:7, separating the rebuke-driven defeat of chariot and horse from the fear-and-judgment sequence, but both stretches sustain the identical second-person address with no intervening vocative shift or Selah, so 76:4-9 read as one continuous strophe.
