rationale: This row begins right after the Selah that closes the preceding unit (web:Ps.76.9 = oshb:Ps.76.10, “סֶֽלָה”), and its own content shifts addressee: rather than continuing the God-directed second-person address of web:Ps.76.4-Ps.76.9, web:Ps.76.11 turns to an imperative addressed to the worshiping community, “Make vows to Yahweh your God, and fulfill them!”, matching “נִֽדֲר֣וּ וְשַׁלְּמוּ֮ לַיהוָ֪ה אֱֽלֹהֵ֫יכֶ֥ם” (oshb:Ps.76.12). Third-person report of divine power then resumes at web:Ps.76.12, “He will cut off the spirit of princes. He is feared by the kings of the earth.” This closes the psalm on the same report register that opened it (web:Ps.76.1 = oshb:Ps.76.2). Yahweh (יהוה) occurs in 1 verse of Psalm 76, this imperative (web:Ps.76.11).

rationale: The opening row carries the title's dual-cite (web:Ps.77.0 = oshb:Ps.77.1); the title's ketiv/qere pair “ידיתון יְדוּת֗וּן” (oshb:Ps.77.1) renders the al-Yeduthun label (“To Jeduthun”, web:Ps.77.0), shared with Psalm 62's title rather than Psalm 39's differently-prefixed one. The psalm opens on a doubled cry, “My cry goes to God! Indeed, I cry to God for help…” (web:Ps.77.1), matching “קוֹלִ֣י אֶל אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְאֶצְעָ֑קָה” (oshb:Ps.77.2), where the phrase for 'my voice to God' repeats within the verse. The distress deepens through web:Ps.77.2 (“In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord… My soul refused to be comforted”) and closes on Selah: “I remember God, and I groan… Selah” (web:Ps.77.3; oshb:Ps.77.4 “אֶזְכְּרָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְאֶֽהֱמָיָ֑ה…סֶֽלָה”).
rejected_alternative: The title could be treated as a bare label carrying no boundary weight of its own, but the brief's owner ruling treats titled-psalm superscriptions as tier-1 opener evidence, so its dual-cite anchors this row's front seam rather than floating free of it.

rationale: The row opens just after the Selah closing the prior unit (web:Ps.77.3 = oshb:Ps.77.4, “סֶֽלָה”), with direct address to God beginning at web:Ps.77.4, “You hold my eyelids open”, then turning reflective at web:Ps.77.5-6 (“I have considered the days of old… I remember my song in the night… my spirit diligently inquires”). That inquiry opens into quoted rhetorical questions at web:Ps.77.7, “Will the Lord reject us forever?”, continuing through web:Ps.77.8 and closing at web:Ps.77.9, “Has God forgotten to be gracious?” Selah closes the row, matching “הֲשָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל…סֶֽלָה” (oshb:Ps.77.10) for the closing pair.
rejected_alternative: The row could split at 77:6/77:7, separating the silent meditation from the quoted despair-questions it introduces, but web:Ps.77.6 ends by announcing the inquiry that web:Ps.77.7-9 then voices in quotation, so the two halves form one continuous movement from reflection to its own quoted content.

rationale: Just past the Selah that closes the quoted despair-questions (web:Ps.77.9 = oshb:Ps.77.10, “סֶֽלָה”), this row opens at the psalm's pivot: “I will appeal to this: the years of the right hand of the Most High” (web:Ps.77.10), matching “שְׁ֝נ֗וֹת יְמִ֣ין עֶלְיֽוֹן” (oshb:Ps.77.11). The meditation turns from complaint to a recital of volitional first-person verbs, “I will remember Yah's deeds… I will also meditate on all your work…” (web:Ps.77.11-12), where the ketiv/qere pair “אזכיר אֶזְכּ֥וֹר” (oshb:Ps.77.12) carries the qere reading 'I will remember/recall'. The recital continues through the incomparability question at web:Ps.77.13 (“What god is great like God?”) and closes on the psalm's third Selah: “You have redeemed your people with your arm, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah” (web:Ps.77.15; oshb:Ps.77.16 “גָּאַ֣לְתָּ בִּזְר֣וֹעַ עַמֶּ֑ךָ בְּנֵי יַעֲקֹ֖ב וְיוֹסֵ֣ף סֶֽלָה”).

The recital's cluster of first-person volitional verbs ('I will remember', 'I will meditate') begins at web:Ps.77.11, favoring 77:10 as the hinge that opens this row rather than the close of the prior one.

rationale: The row opens just after the Selah closing the recital of wonders (web:Ps.77.15 = oshb:Ps.77.16, “סֶֽלָה”), shifting register from confessional address to vivid theophany description: “The waters saw you, God. The waters saw you, and they writhed” (web:Ps.77.16), matching “רָ֘א֤וּךָ מַּ֨יִם אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים רָא֣וּךָ מַּ֣יִם יָחִ֑ילוּ” (oshb:Ps.77.17), with the clause repeated within the verse. Storm imagery continues through web:Ps.77.17-18 (“The clouds poured out water… The voice of your thunder was in the whirlwind…”) and the sea-crossing motif at web:Ps.77.19 (“Your way was through the sea… Your footsteps were not known”), before the psalm ends at web:Ps.77.20, “You led your people like a flock, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” The Hebrew reads “בְּֽיַד מֹשֶׁ֥ה וְאַהֲרֹֽן” (oshb:Ps.77.21). No doxology, refrain, or return to direct address follows the Moses/Aaron notice; the psalm closes on the narrative image itself.
rejected_alternative: The theophany could be kept with the preceding recital as one long web:Ps.77.10-Ps.77.20 unit, since both stretches recount Yah's deeds, but the shift from first-person confessional verbs ('I will remember/meditate') to third-person-addressed nature imagery ('the waters saw you') at web:Ps.77.16 is a register change independent of the Selah that closes web:Ps.77.15, so the theophany is kept as its own row.

rationale: Psalm 78 opens with a maskil superscription (“A contemplation by Asaph.”, web:Ps.78.0) sitting inside the same MT verse as the psalm's opening imperative, then unfolds one continuous wisdom exordium: the call “Hear my teaching, my people. Turn your ears to the words of my mouth.” (web:Ps.78.1) sets a teacher's address that a purpose-clause chain develops — the covenant-transmission command of web:Ps.78.5, extended by “that the generation to come might know…who should arise and tell their children” (web:Ps.78.6) and “that they might set their hope in God, and not forget God's deeds, but keep his commandments” (web:Ps.78.7) — until it resolves in a negative exemplar, “and might not be as their fathers- a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation that didn't make their hearts loyal, whose spirit was not steadfast with God.” (web:Ps.78.8). The unnamed “fathers” of web:Ps.78.8 are then given a specific referent at web:Ps.78.9, marking the seam.
rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.78.4's transmission pledge was considered but rejected because the purpose clauses of web:Ps.78.5-web:Ps.78.7 continue the same sentence movement toward the negative paradigm at web:Ps.78.8.

device_notes: Every row below answers to one parent: Psalm 78. Its title carries the maskil and le-Asaph genre labels (web:Ps.78.0 = oshb:Ps.78.1).

rationale: The frame's unnamed negative exemplar is instantiated by name: “The children of Ephraim, being armed and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle.” (web:Ps.78.9) opens a three-verse indictment that generalizes from that one tribal failure to covenant-breaking at large — “They didn't keep God's covenant, and refused to walk in his law.” (web:Ps.78.10) — and closes on forgetting, “They forgot his doings, his wondrous deeds that he had shown them.” (web:Ps.78.11), which is exactly what the historical recital opening at web:Ps.78.12 sets out to remedy. The named tribe recurs at the psalm's close (web:Ps.78.67), where the same Ephraim is explicitly passed over for Judah.
rejected_alternative: That alternative — folding these three verses into the historical recital that follows — does not hold: web:Ps.78.9-web:Ps.78.11 stay in the summary-indictment register of web:Ps.78.8 rather than the itemized narrative register that opens at web:Ps.78.12.

rationale: Psalm 82 is chunked as one parent unit spanning its full row. rationale: Psalm 84 stands as one liturgical composition; its rows group under one parent. The strophe moves from the psalmist's own longing (“My soul longs, and even faints for the courts of Yahweh”, web:Ps.84.2) through the sparrow-and-swallow figure (web:Ps.84.3) to a beatitude that universalizes the longing onto “those who dwell in your house” (web:Ps.84.4), oshb:Ps.84.5's opening “אַ֭שְׁרֵי יוֹשְׁבֵ֣י בֵיתֶ֑ךָ” — the first of a three-fold ashrei formula recurring at web:Ps.84.5 and web:Ps.84.12 (sweep: 3 verses in Psalm 84, skeleton ashrei, 31 book-wide). Selah closes the strophe at web:Ps.84.4 (oshb:Ps.84.5).

rationale: One parent spans Psalm 85's rows. rationale: All rows of this psalm belong to a single parent unit. the unit’s content moves from relational dwelling-place language (90:1) to the fixed phrase ‘from everlasting to everlasting’ (90:2), both predicated of Yahweh/God
device_notes: One parent, Psalm 90, holds all of this prayer’s rows together as a single composition.

rationale: Human transience displaces divine eternity as the subject: “You turn man to destruction, saying, "Return, you children of men."” (web:Ps.90.3) sets the theme, developed through a timescale comparison — “a thousand years in your sight are just like yesterday… like a watch in the night” (web:Ps.90.4) — then the grass metaphor: swept away in sleep, sprouting in the morning, “By evening, it is withered and dry” (web:Ps.90.6).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the ‘return, you children of men’ saying (90:3) from the timescale and grass images (90:4-6) into two rows was considered, but both illustrate the same theme that 90:3 announces, with no addressee or mode break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative-within-quotation ‘Return’ (shuvu) opens the transience theme at 90:3
two illustrations of the same theme (timescale, 90:4; grass, 90:5-6) run without a further mode shift

rationale: A causal connective binds mortality to divine wrath as its explanation: “For we are consumed in your anger. We are troubled in your wrath” (web:Ps.90.7) names sin as the cause (web:Ps.90.8) and totals the lifespan — “seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years” (web:Ps.90.10) — before the unit closes on the wisdom petition its own meditation earns: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (web:Ps.90.12).
rejected_alternative: Carrying this unit through 90:13 so that the wisdom petition and the plea to relent form one row was considered, but 90:13 opens with its own fresh imperative (‘Relent, Yahweh’) distinct from the reflective ‘teach us’ request that closes this unit.
observed_substrate_signals: ki (‘for’) opens 90:7 as a causal connective tying the wrath-theme to the preceding transience images
the unit’s own close (90:12) is a request for wisdom, not yet the imperative petition series that follows

rationale: The psalm’s closing petition opens on a fresh imperative: “Relent, Yahweh! How long? Have compassion on your servants!” (שׁוּבָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה עַד מָתָ֑י…, web:Ps.90.13 = oshb:Ps.90.13), moving through the plea to be satisfied “in the morning with your loving kindness” (web:Ps.90.14) and for gladness proportioned to the years of affliction (web:Ps.90.15), to the psalm’s own final request, repeated for emphasis: “Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands” (web:Ps.90.17).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the petition at 90:15/16, separating the gladness-request from the work-of-our-hands request, was considered, but the imperative sequence (satisfy, make glad, let appear, establish) runs without an addressee or mode break across the whole unit.
observed_substrate_signals: shuvah (‘return/relent’), an imperative opening a fresh petition at 90:13, echoes the shuvu (‘return’) addressed to ‘the children of men’ at 90:3, tier-2 verbal-root echo
the closing request (90:17) repeats ‘establish the work of our hands’ within the same verse for emphasis, the unit’s own final imperative

rationale: The psalm opens in third-person description, “He who dwells…” (web:Ps.91.1), before the voice turns to first-person confession, “I will say of…” (web:Ps.91.2), whose object clause WEB itself closes inside quotation marks at the end of the verse. The second-person address that runs from web:Ps.91.3 onward has not yet opened, so the opening description and its confession stand together as one unit before the address begins.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.91.3 shifts both grammatical person and addressee, opening the protective second-person address that governs the rest of the psalm rather than continuing the speaker's own confession, so folding it into this row was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.91.1's opening participle יֹ֭שֵׁב (oshb:Ps.91.1, 'dwells') names a generic figure, not an addressed 'you'
WEB's own quotation marks close the confession within web:Ps.91.2, one verse before the second-person address opens
device_notes: Rows of Psalm 91 group to one parent unit.

rationale: From web:Ps.91.3 the psalm addresses a singular 'you' directly, cataloguing dangers the addressee is protected from -- snare, pestilence, terror by night, the arrow by day -- through web:Ps.91.8, then restates the premise of that protection, “Because you have made Yahweh your…” (web:Ps.91.9), and its result, “no evil shall happen…” (web:Ps.91.10). This eight-verse span holds one continuous second-person address before a new governing image -- the angels of web:Ps.91.11 -- opens the next unit.
rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.91.9, where the refuge premise is restated, was rejected because vv.9-10 supply the reason and result for the preceding danger catalogue rather than opening a new topic.
observed_substrate_signals: the addressee is carried throughout vv.3-10 by second-person suffixed pronouns rather than a fresh independent pronoun or new grammatical subject
web:Ps.91.10's closing clause answers web:Ps.91.9's premise within the same span
device_notes: No superscription or refrain marking touches this span, and no selah falls within it either; the danger catalogue forms one continuous address unit, distinct from the psalm's other spans.

rationale: web:Ps.91.11 introduces a new grammatical subject, כִּ֣י מַ֭לְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה לָּ֑ךְ (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'for his angels he will command for you'), naming the specific agent of protection rather than the generic dangers of the preceding span; the angelic guardianship carries through web:Ps.91.13's triumph over the lion and serpent, before the voice shifts again to Yahweh's own first-person speech at web:Ps.91.14.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.91.14 introduces a first-person divine speaker, a distinct voice from the third-person angels of vv.11-13, so carrying this span forward into it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: מַ֭לְאָכָיו (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'his angels') is the span's own grammatical subject, distinct from the implied dangers of the previous span
device_notes: The angelic-guardianship image is local to this span; it does not recur elsewhere in the psalm.

rationale: web:Ps.91.14 opens with the causal clause כִּ֤י בִ֣י חָ֭שַׁק וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'because he has clung to me and I will deliver him'), a first-person divine verb shifting the speaker from the address-voice of vv.3-13 to Yahweh's own voice; WEB marks the shift with its own quotation mark, opening “Because he has set his love on me,…” (web:Ps.91.14) and closing “…show him my salvation.” (web:Ps.91.16) at the psalm's end. This closing oracle, in which God speaks of the trusting individual in the third person ('him'), is a distinct unit from the second-person address that precedes it.
rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.91.13 as the oracle's opening verse was rejected because it still addresses 'you' in the second person, while web:Ps.91.14 is where Yahweh's own first-person voice begins.
observed_substrate_signals: WEB brackets this span in its own quotation marks, opening at web:Ps.91.14 and closing at web:Ps.91.16, the psalm's final verse
the verb וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'and I will deliver him') is first-person, unlike the third-person and second-person verbs of the rest of the psalm
device_notes: The closing oracle carries the psalm's direct divine first-person speech, distinct in voice from its other three spans.

rationale: The title, מִזְמ֥וֹר שִׁ֗יר לְי֣וֹם הַשַּׁבָּֽת (oshb:Ps.92.1, 'a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day'), names this psalm for the Sabbath -- “A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.” (web:Ps.92.0) is the book's only WEB title to do so (sweep: 1 verse, book-wide 'Sabbath' search over WEB titles and text). Three parallel infinitive clauses then open the body -- to give thanks, to proclaim loving kindness, and to play the instruments named at web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 -- forming one syntactic unit that the causal 'For you, Yahweh' of web:Ps.92.4 breaks off from.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.92.4 leaves the infinitive chain of thanksgiving-instructions for a direct second-person address to Yahweh, so extending this row through it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: the genre_label_membership inventory records this psalm under both mizmor and shir, matching the title's own two nouns
web:Ps.92.1 = oshb:Ps.92.2 through web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 form one infinitive chain governed by 'It is a good thing' (web:Ps.92.1)
device_notes: Psalm 92 serves as parent for the rows it contains.

rationale: web:Ps.92.4 = oshb:Ps.92.5 opens with כִּ֤י שִׂמַּחְתַּ֣נִי יְהוָ֣ה ('for you have made me glad, Yahweh'), a direct second-person address that continues through “How great are your works, Yahweh!” (web:Ps.92.5 = oshb:Ps.92.6); the reflection on Yahweh's works then turns to what the senseless fail to grasp -- that the wicked, though they flourish, will be destroyed forever (web:Ps.92.6 = oshb:Ps.92.7; web:Ps.92.7 = oshb:Ps.92.8) -- before the adversative 'But you' of web:Ps.92.8 resumes direct address.
rejected_alternative: Splitting web:Ps.92.6-Ps.92.7 into its own row was rejected because the fool's failure to understand (web:Ps.92.6) is completed by naming what he fails to understand (web:Ps.92.7), one clause continuing the other.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.92.5 opens with the causal כִּ֤י ('for'), pivoting from the preceding infinitive chain to a finite, addressed clause
device_notes: The wicked's transience (web:Ps.92.7) is offered as the content of what the senseless fail to grasp (web:Ps.92.6), one wisdom-styled unit inside the hymn.

rationale: web:Ps.92.8 = oshb:Ps.92.9 opens with the adversative independent pronoun וְאַתָּ֥ה מָר֗וֹם ('but you, on high'), turning back to direct address after the wisdom reflection of vv.6-7; the enemies' perishing (web:Ps.92.9) and the psalmist's own exaltation and anointing (web:Ps.92.10-Ps.92.11) follow as one address-governed unit, closed off when the fronted, unaddressed subject 'the righteous' opens web:Ps.92.12.
rejected_alternative: Separating the enemies' perishing (web:Ps.92.9) from the psalmist's exaltation (web:Ps.92.10-Ps.92.11) was rejected because both remain inside the same second-person-address frame opened at web:Ps.92.8, without a fresh addressee or subject marking a seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: וְאַתָּ֥ה מָר֗וֹם (oshb:Ps.92.9) is an explicit independent pronoun, distinct from the bound suffixes used elsewhere in the psalm
web:Ps.92.12 = oshb:Ps.92.13 opens with the fronted subject צַ֭דִּיק כַּתָּמָ֣ר יִפְרָ֑ח ('the righteous shall flourish'), a topic shift out of this row's address
device_notes: The horn-exaltation image (web:Ps.92.10) is local to this span.

rationale: web:Ps.92.12 = oshb:Ps.92.13 opens with the fronted, unaddressed subject צַ֭דִּיק כַּתָּמָ֣ר יִפְרָ֑ח ('the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree'), leaving the second-person address of the preceding span for a third-person, gnomic image of the righteous planted in Yahweh's house (web:Ps.92.13) and still bearing fruit in old age (web:Ps.92.14); the psalm closes on the purpose clause “to show that Yahweh is upright.” (web:Ps.92.15).
rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.92.12 attached to the preceding span was rejected because it drops the second-person address entirely for a generalized class statement about 'the righteous,' a fresh grammatical subject rather than a continuation of 'you.'
observed_substrate_signals: the tree image (palm, cedar) and the temple-courts setting recur across vv.12-14 as one continuous figure, absent from the preceding span
device_notes: The closing verse's purpose clause (web:Ps.92.15) restates the psalm's opening claim that giving thanks to Yahweh is 'a good thing' (web:Ps.92.1), an inclusio in theme rather than repeated wording.

rationale: The psalm opens “Yahweh reigns!” (web:Ps.93.1), the verb clause יְהוָ֣ה מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1, 'Yahweh has become king') -- sweep: the skeleton יהוה מלך returns 6 verses book-wide (web:Ps.10.16, web:Ps.29.10, web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1), but the pointed verb מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1), distinct from the noun מֶ֭לֶךְ (oshb:Ps.10.16, 'king', in 'Yahweh is king forever and ever'), narrows the 6 to 4 verses carrying the verb (web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1: sweep, 4 verses); web:Ps.93.1 precedes the other 3, making this the book's first YHWH-malak proclamation of the 4 (sweep, 4 verses). Five verses carry one continuous enthronement acclamation, from the throne 'established from long ago' (web:Ps.93.2) through the flood's roar (web:Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4) to the closing statement that “Your statutes stand firm.” (web:Ps.93.5); at five verses the whole psalm holds as one indivisible unit with no address or speaker change marking an internal seam.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the psalm at web:Ps.93.2, separating the enthronement acclamation from the throne's antiquity, was rejected because the whole five verses form one uninterrupted hymn with no addressee change or internal quotation to mark a seam.
observed_substrate_signals: מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1) is a finite qal perfect verb, opening the psalm before any addressee is named
the psalm's five verses carry no second-person address and no internal quotation
device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition -- parent grouping Psalm 93.

rationale: The psalm opens with an imperative appeal to the avenging God, אֵל נְקָמ֥וֹת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.94.1, 'God of vengeance, Yahweh'), continuing in direct address through “Yahweh, how long will…” (web:Ps.94.3); the complaint then turns to third-person description of the wicked's deeds -- oppressing the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless (web:Ps.94.5-Ps.94.6) -- and closes on their own quoted boast, “Yah will not see, neither will Jacob’s God consider.” (web:Ps.94.7). This seven-verse complaint ends before the imperative rebuke of the 'senseless' opens a new addressee at web:Ps.94.8.
rejected_alternative: Ending the row at web:Ps.94.4, where the wicked's arrogant words are named, was rejected because their specific acts (vv.5-6) and their quoted boast (v.7) continue the same complaint without a new addressee or speaker.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.94.1 opens with a doubled vocative, אֵל נְקָמ֥וֹת (oshb:Ps.94.1) named twice in the verse, an intensified invocation
the wicked's own words are quoted at the close of this span (web:Ps.94.7), not before it
device_notes: Psalm 94 supplies the parent for its strophes.

rationale: web:Ps.94.8 opens with the imperative בִּ֭ינוּ בֹּעֲרִ֣ים בָּעָ֑ם (oshb:Ps.94.8, 'consider, you dullards among the people'), addressing the senseless and the fools directly rather than Yahweh -- a wisdom-instruction register distinct from the preceding complaint. The rebuke's rhetorical questions (web:Ps.94.9-Ps.94.11) give way to a beatitude, “Blessed is the man” (web:Ps.94.12), on the man Yahweh disciplines, and the span closes on the promise that judgment 'will return to righteousness' (web:Ps.94.15); the rhetorical 'who' of web:Ps.94.16 then reopens the psalm in the first person, marking this eight-verse wisdom-instruction stretch as the psalm's internal seam between the opening complaint and the closing personal appeal.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the rebuke of the fools (vv.8-11) from the beatitude on the disciplined man (vv.12-15) was rejected because both remain in the same wisdom-instruction register, addressed to a general audience rather than to Yahweh or in the first person.
observed_substrate_signals: אַשְׁרֵ֤י (oshb:Ps.94.12, 'blessed') is a fixed macarism formula, not repeated elsewhere within this span
device_notes: The rebuke-then-beatitude pairing is a common wisdom-psalm move (the fool addressed, then the disciplined man blessed); it is texture within this span, not a further row boundary.

rationale: web:Ps.94.16 reopens the psalm in the first person, “Who will rise up for…” (web:Ps.94.16), a personal testimony -- Yahweh as help (web:Ps.94.17), comfort amid anxious thoughts (web:Ps.94.19) -- that gives way to a renewed second-person address to Yahweh about the 'throne of wickedness' at web:Ps.94.20, then closes on the psalm's final declaration, “Yahweh, our God, will cut them off.” (web:Ps.94.23). This eight-verse span carries the psalm from personal testimony to its concluding confidence, with no further addressee change strong enough to mark an internal boundary.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at web:Ps.94.20, where the address turns back to Yahweh, was rejected because the surrounding first-person testimony (vv.16-19, 22) and the address to Yahweh (v.20) share the same complaint against 'the throne of wickedness' without a change of topic.
observed_substrate_signals: מִֽי (oshb:Ps.94.16, 'who') opens a rhetorical question absent from the wisdom-instruction span that precedes it
הַֽ֭יְחָבְרְךָ (oshb:Ps.94.20, an interrogative-prefixed verb bearing a second-person suffix) briefly returns to direct address inside this span, noted as texture rather than a row boundary
device_notes: web:Ps.94.23 repeats its closing verb ('will cut them off') before naming 'Yahweh, our God,' an intensifying repetition distinct from the doubled 'God of vengeance' invocation that opens the psalm at web:Ps.94.1.

rationale: The psalm opens with the imperative לְ֭כוּ נְרַנְּנָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.1, 'come, let us sing'), “Oh come, let’s sing to Yahweh.” (web:Ps.95.1), continuing in the same imperative-plural voice with נְקַדְּמָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.2, 'let us come before') through “Let’s come before his presence with thanksgiving.” (web:Ps.95.2); the causal 'For' opening web:Ps.95.3 shifts from imperative summons to the grounds for it, closing this two-verse call to worship as one unit.
rejected_alternative: Extending this row through web:Ps.95.3 was rejected because that verse leaves the imperative-plural summons for a causal clause giving the grounds for worship.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.95.1 and oshb:Ps.95.2 both open with imperative or cohortative-plural forms (לְ֭כוּ, נְקַדְּמָ֣ה), a pairing distinct from web:Ps.95.3's causal opener
device_notes: Every row below answers to the same parent, Psalm 95.

rationale: web:Ps.95.3 opens with the causal כִּ֤י אֵ֣ל גָּד֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.95.3, 'for Yahweh is a great God'), giving the grounds for the preceding summons in a hymn of creation that names the deep places of the earth, the mountain heights (web:Ps.95.4), and the sea Yahweh made with his own hands (web:Ps.95.5); the second imperative 'Oh come, let's worship' at web:Ps.95.6 opens a fresh summons, closing this three-verse causal unit.
rejected_alternative: web:Ps.95.6 returns to the imperative register of vv.1-2 rather than continuing the causal, descriptive clauses of vv.3-5, so carrying this row through it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּ֤י (oshb:Ps.95.3, 'for') is the span's own causal opener, with no further כי-clause before web:Ps.95.6's return to the imperative
device_notes: The creation imagery (deep places, mountains, sea) is local to this span.

rationale: web:Ps.95.6 opens a second imperative summons, בֹּ֭אוּ נִשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.6, 'come, let us bow down'), “Oh come, let’s worship and bow down.” (web:Ps.95.6), grounded in the covenant self-identification 'we are the people of his pasture' (web:Ps.95.7); the verse then pivots on its own closing clause, “Today, oh that you would hear his voice!” (web:Ps.95.7), into the oath-oracle that follows at web:Ps.95.8, closing this two-verse summons-and-pivot unit before Yahweh's own first-person voice opens.
rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.95.7's closing clause into the following oracle span was rejected because the clause is still spoken by the worship leader urging the congregation to listen, not yet Yahweh's own first-person speech, which begins at web:Ps.95.8.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.95.6 echoes web:Ps.95.1's opening imperative with a second, distinct verb of coming, pairing the two summonses that bracket the psalm's opening praise
device_notes: web:Ps.95.7's closing exhortation, 'Today, if you would hear his voice,' is the psalm's own lead-in to the oracle that follows.

rationale: web:Ps.95.8 opens “Don’t harden your heart,” (web:Ps.95.8), naming כִּמְרִיבָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.95.8, 'Meribah') and כְּי֥וֹם מַ֝סָּ֗ה (oshb:Ps.95.8, 'the day of Massah'); the first-person verb-suffixes נִ֭סּוּנִי and בְּ֝חָנ֗וּנִי (oshb:Ps.95.9, 'tested me', 'proved me') retroactively identify the speaker as Yahweh rather than the worship leader, so this rebuke belongs to the same oracle as “Forty long years” (web:Ps.95.10), naming אַרְבָּ֘עִ֤ים שָׁנָ֨ה (oshb:Ps.95.10, 'forty years'), and the closing oath, “Therefore I swore…” (web:Ps.95.11). The oracle runs to the psalm's closing verse, ending this four-verse unit.
rejected_alternative: Opening the oracle at web:Ps.95.9 alone, where the first-person object suffixes unambiguously mark Yahweh as speaker, was rejected because web:Ps.95.8's rebuke and web:Ps.95.9's account of the fathers' testing form one uninterrupted sentence in the Hebrew, with no intervening verb of speech to mark a new speaker mid-clause.
observed_substrate_signals: נִ֭סּוּנִי and בְּ֝חָנ֗וּנִי (oshb:Ps.95.9) carry first-person object suffixes (-ni, 'me'), marking Yahweh as the oracle's speaker
no Selah or other disclosure-inventory mark falls within this span (pmarks_Ps.json)
device_notes: The Meribah/Massah rebellion (web:Ps.95.8) is not named elsewhere across this part's 70 verses (sweep: 70 verses, Ps.91-95).

rationale: Psalm 96 stands as one liturgical composition; its rows group under one parent. The strophe opens with the doubled summons “Sing to Yahweh a new song! Sing to Yahweh, all the earth.” (web:Ps.96.1; byte: שִׁ֣ירוּ לַ֭יהוָה שִׁ֣יר חָדָ֑שׁ, oshb:Ps.96.1), widens through the missionary imperative “Declare his glory among the nations” (web:Ps.96.3), and turns causal at web:Ps.96.4 (“For Yahweh is great, and greatly to be praised!”), a grounding clause that runs through the sanctuary description closing web:Ps.96.6. A fresh vocative imperative cluster reopens the address at web:Ps.96.7 (“Ascribe to Yahweh, you families of nations”; byte: הָב֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת עַמִּ֑ים, oshb:Ps.96.7), so the strophe boundary sits at 96:6|96:7.
rejected_alternative: Closing this unit at 96:3, right after the opening imperative burst, was rejected because the causal clause opening web:Ps.96.4 continues rather than answers that same summons.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: שִׁ֣ירוּ לַ֭יהוָה שִׁ֣יר חָדָ֑שׁ (oshb:Ps.96.1) opens the psalm with a doubled sing-imperative toward “all the earth”.
byte: הָב֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת עַמִּ֑ים (oshb:Ps.96.7) reopens the vocative address to the nations' families, marking the strophe close at 96:6|96:7.
device_notes: The opening clause “Sing to Yahweh a new song” (web:Ps.96.1; byte: שִׁ֣ירוּ לַ֭יהוָה שִׁ֣יר חָדָ֑שׁ, oshb:Ps.96.1) shares its first four Hebrew words with the opening of web:Ps.98.1 (byte: שִׁ֤ירוּ לַֽיהוָ֨ה שִׁ֣יר, oshb:Ps.98.1; skeleton sweep: 2 verses carry this exact four-word new-song clause within this span, 96:1 and 98:1), though the two continuations diverge right after the shared clause: 96:1 repeats the sing-imperative toward “all the earth” (web:Ps.96.1) while 98:1 turns to a causal “for he has done marvelous things” (web:Ps.98.1).

rationale: The imperative cluster opened at web:Ps.96.7 runs through the worship call of web:Ps.96.9 (“Worship Yahweh in holy array. Tremble before him, all the earth.”), then the register shifts from imperative to declarative at web:Ps.96.10 with the embedded proclamation “Yahweh reigns.” (byte: אִמְר֤וּ בַגּוֹיִ֨ם יְה֘וָ֤ה מָלָ֗ךְ, oshb:Ps.96.10), and from there into the cosmic jussives of web:Ps.96.11-96.12 (“Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice.”) that resolve in the closing judgment formula of web:Ps.96.13 (“He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.”; byte: לִפְנֵ֤י יְהוָ֨ה כִּ֬י בָ֗א כִּ֥י בָא֮ לִשְׁפֹּ֪ט הָ֫אָ֥רֶץ יִשְׁפֹּֽט תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּצֶ֑דֶק וְ֝עַמִּ֗ים בֶּאֱמוּנָתֽוֹ, oshb:Ps.96.13).
rejected_alternative: Splitting off 96:10 alone as its own row was rejected: the kingship proclamation sits inside the same imperative-to-cosmic movement as 96:7-9 and 96:11-13, with no independent seam marker isolating it.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: אִמְר֤וּ בַגּוֹיִ֨ם יְה֘וָ֤ה מָלָ֗ךְ (oshb:Ps.96.10) carries the יהוה מלך kingship clause embedded as reported speech inside ‘say among the nations’, one of two attested clause forms of this proclamation in this span (sweep: 3 verses, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1; the third occurrence is at web:Ps.93.1, outside this span).
No selah occurs across this span (pmarks_Ps.json inventory; span-scoped absence).

rationale: All rows of this psalm belong to a single parent unit. The strophe opens with the standalone proclamation “Yahweh reigns! Let the earth rejoice! Let the multitude of islands be glad!” (web:Ps.97.1; byte: יְהוָ֣ה מָ֭לָךְ תָּגֵ֣ל הָאָ֑רֶץ, oshb:Ps.97.1) and moves straight into theophany imagery — clouds, darkness, fire, and melting mountains — through web:Ps.97.2-97.5, closing this movement where the heavens themselves become witness at web:Ps.97.6 (“The heavens declare his righteousness.”). The address shifts at web:Ps.97.7 from cosmic description to an imperative aimed at idol-worshippers, marking the strophe boundary at 97:6|97:7.
rejected_alternative: A shorter opening ending at 97:4 was rejected because the mountain-melting image of web:Ps.97.5 completes rather than opens a new clause of the same theophany.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: יְהוָ֣ה מָ֭לָךְ תָּגֵ֣ל הָאָ֑רֶץ (oshb:Ps.97.1) opens with the יהוה מלך clause as a verse-initial independent declaration, the same clause form as web:Ps.99.1 (sweep: 2 verses share this verse-initial form in this span).

rationale: The strophe opens with the imperative “Let all them be shamed who serve engraved images” (web:Ps.97.7; byte: יֵבֹ֤שׁוּ כָּל עֹ֬בְדֵי פֶ֗סֶל, oshb:Ps.97.7), aimed at idol-worshippers, then follows Zion's glad response at web:Ps.97.8 (“Zion heard and was glad.”) into direct address to Yahweh at web:Ps.97.9 (“For you, Yahweh, are most high above all the earth.”). The address turns back to the congregation at web:Ps.97.10 with a fresh imperative, “You who love Yahweh, hate evil!”, running through the closing exhortation of web:Ps.97.12 (“Give thanks to his holy Name.”).
rejected_alternative: Treating 97:9 as its own row was rejected because the direct address to Yahweh answers rather than interrupts the idol-shame imperative opened at 97:7.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: יֵבֹ֤שׁוּ כָּל עֹ֬בְדֵי פֶ֗סֶל (oshb:Ps.97.7) opens this unit's imperative addressed to idol-worshippers, distinct in addressee from the theophany description closing the prior strophe at 97:6.

rationale: The psalm coheres as one composition — parent grouping Psalm 98. Its title sits inside MT v1 (“A Psalm.”, web:Ps.98.0 = oshb:Ps.98.1; byte: מִזְמ֡וֹר), immediately followed by the new-song summons “Sing to Yahweh a new song” (web:Ps.98.1; byte: מִזְמ֡וֹר שִׁ֤ירוּ לַֽיהוָ֨ה שִׁ֣יר חָ֭דָשׁ, oshb:Ps.98.1) and its causal ground, “for he has done marvelous things!”. Third-person narration of Yahweh's acts runs through web:Ps.98.2-98.3, closing on “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” (web:Ps.98.3). The register shifts to imperative at web:Ps.98.4, marking the strophe boundary at 98:3|98:4.
rejected_alternative: Folding 98:1-9 into one whole-psalm row was rejected: the narration of 98:1-3 and the imperative-plus-cosmic movement of 98:4-9 stay internally uniform in grammatical person, an independent tier-1 seam at 98:3|98:4.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: מִזְמ֡וֹר (oshb:Ps.98.1) stands as this title's genre-label word on its own; the superscription carries no second label word before the verse's own content begins.

byte: מִזְמ֡וֹר שִׁ֤ירוּ לַֽיהוָ֨ה שִׁ֣יר חָ֭דָשׁ (oshb:Ps.98.1) opens with the same four-word new-song clause as web:Ps.96.1 (byte: שִׁ֣ירוּ לַ֭יהוָה שִׁ֣יר חָדָ֑שׁ, oshb:Ps.96.1); see the typed relation at 96's opening row.

rationale: The imperative “Make a joyful noise to Yahweh, all the earth!” (web:Ps.98.4; byte: הָרִ֣יעוּ לַֽ֭יהוָה כָּל הָאָ֑רֶץ, oshb:Ps.98.4) opens a call to instrumental praise — harp, trumpet, and ram's horn — through web:Ps.98.6, then turns to cosmic imperatives (sea, rivers, mountains) in web:Ps.98.7-98.8, closing on the judgment formula of web:Ps.98.9 (“He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.”; byte: לִֽפְֽנֵי יְהוָ֗ה כִּ֥י בָא֮ לִשְׁפֹּ֪ט הָ֫אָ֥רֶץ יִשְׁפֹּֽט תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּצֶ֑דֶק וְ֝עַמִּ֗ים בְּמֵישָׁרִֽים, oshb:Ps.98.9).
rejected_alternative: Claiming this closing formula matched web:Ps.96.13's closing formula word-for-word was rejected: collated at byte tier (sweep: 2 verses compared, 96:13 and 98:9) the two diverge (96:13 doubles ‘for he comes’ and closes on ‘his truth’ while 98:9 closes on ‘equity’, matching 96:10's own wording instead).
observed_substrate_signals: byte: לִֽפְֽנֵי יְהוָ֗ה כִּ֥י בָא֮ לִשְׁפֹּ֪ט הָ֫אָ֥רֶץ יִשְׁפֹּֽט תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּצֶ֑דֶק וְ֝עַמִּ֗ים בְּמֵישָׁרִֽים (oshb:Ps.98.9) parallels but does not collate byte-identical to לִפְנֵ֤י יְהוָ֨ה כִּ֬י בָ֗א כִּ֥י בָא֮ לִשְׁפֹּ֪ט הָ֫אָ֥רֶץ יִשְׁפֹּֽט תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּצֶ֑דֶק וְ֝עַמִּ֗ים בֶּאֱמוּנָתֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.96.13) (collate: 2 verses compared); 98:9 lacks 96:13's doubled ‘for he comes’ and closes on a different final word.

rationale: One parent spans Psalm 99's rows. The strophe opens with the verse-initial proclamation “Yahweh reigns! Let the peoples tremble.” (web:Ps.99.1; byte: יְהוָ֣ה מָ֭לָךְ יִרְגְּז֣וּ עַמִּ֑ים, oshb:Ps.99.1), continues “Yahweh is great in Zion.” at web:Ps.99.2, and closes its opening movement on the refrain “He is Holy!” (web:Ps.99.3; byte: קָד֥וֹשׁ הֽוּא, oshb:Ps.99.3).
rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 99:5 to gather both early refrain instances into one row was rejected: web:Ps.99.4 opens a distinct royal-justice clause addressed in second person, an independent driver for a new strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: יְהוָ֣ה מָ֭לָךְ יִרְגְּז֣וּ עַמִּ֑ים (oshb:Ps.99.1) opens with the same verse-initial יהוה מלך clause form as web:Ps.97.1 (sweep: 2 verses share this form in this span; a third, differently-formed instance sits at web:Ps.96.10).

rationale: The King's justice is named directly at web:Ps.99.4 (“The King’s strength also loves justice.”), a second-person address (“You establish equity.”) distinct from the third-person opening of the prior strophe. The imperative “Exalt Yahweh our God.” opens web:Ps.99.5 and the unit closes on the refrain's second instance, “He is Holy!” (web:Ps.99.5; byte: קָד֥וֹשׁ הֽוּא, oshb:Ps.99.5), byte-identical to the refrain closing web:Ps.99.3 (collate: 2 verses match at byte tier, 99:3 and 99:5).
rejected_alternative: Merging 99:4 into the preceding strophe was rejected because its second-person address to Yahweh about royal justice has no antecedent vocative in 99:1-3, which stays third-person throughout.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: קָד֥וֹשׁ הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.99.5) collates byte-identical to קָד֥וֹשׁ הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.99.3) (collate: 2 verses match), the same two-word refrain closing both verses.

rationale: The strophe turns to historical recollection at web:Ps.99.6 (“Moses and Aaron were among his priests”), naming Moses, Aaron, and Samuel through web:Ps.99.7, then shifts to direct second-person address at web:Ps.99.8 (“You answered them, Yahweh our God.”), and closes on the refrain's third instance at web:Ps.99.9, which widens its wording rather than repeating the earlier refrain word-for-word: “for Yahweh, our God, is holy!” (byte: כִּֽי קָ֝ד֗וֹשׁ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽינוּ, oshb:Ps.99.9) replaces the closing pronoun of 99:3 and 99:5 with an explicit repetition of the divine name and title.
rejected_alternative: Reading 99:9 as a fourth verbatim repetition of the 99:3/99:5 refrain was rejected: collated at byte tier the closing words differ, so the return corroborates the strophe's close without matching the earlier refrain word-for-word.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: כִּֽי קָ֝ד֗וֹשׁ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽינוּ (oshb:Ps.99.9) is the third and final holy-refrain return in this psalm; unlike the byte-identical pair at 99:3/99:5 (oshb:Ps.99.3), it substitutes a longer causal clause naming Yahweh directly for the shorter two-word refrain form.

rationale: Psalm 100 is sung as a single unbroken unit; one parent covers its span. Its title sits inside MT v1 (“A Psalm of thanksgiving.”, web:Ps.100.0 = oshb:Ps.100.1; byte: מִזְמ֥וֹר לְתוֹדָ֑ה), and the five verses move as one uninterrupted call: the summons “Shout for joy to Yahweh, all you lands!” (web:Ps.100.1), the service imperative of web:Ps.100.2, the confession “Know that Yahweh, he is God.” (web:Ps.100.3), the temple-entry imperative of web:Ps.100.4, and the closing motive clause “For Yahweh is good. His loving kindness endures forever, his faithfulness to all generations.” (web:Ps.100.5). No internal seam in this five-verse span carries independent tier-1 support strong enough to divide it.
rejected_alternative: Splitting at 100:2|100:3 to separate the imperative call from the confession was rejected: web:Ps.100.3's confession still addresses the same congregation summoned in 100:1-2 with no vocative or addressee change.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: ולא וְל֣וֹ (oshb:Ps.100.3) straddles a ketiv/qere pair — ketiv reads ‘and not’, qere reads ‘and his’ — disclosed per the kq inventory (pmarks_Ps.json).
No selah occurs in this psalm's five verses (pmarks_Ps.json inventory; span-scoped absence).

rationale: A single parent binds every row of Psalm 101 together. Its title sits inside MT v1 (“A Psalm by David.”, web:Ps.101.0 = oshb:Ps.101.1; byte: לְדָוִ֗ד מִ֫זְמ֥וֹר), opening a first-person vow, “I will sing of loving kindness and justice.” (web:Ps.101.1), that turns to personal resolve at web:Ps.101.2 (“I will be careful to live a blameless life.”; byte: אַשְׂכִּ֤ילָה בְּדֶ֬רֶךְ תָּמִ֗ים, oshb:Ps.101.2) and continues through web:Ps.101.3-101.4's rejection of ‘vile thing’ and ‘perverse heart’ as matters of the psalmist's own household and eyes.
rejected_alternative: Reading all 8 verses of this psalm as one whole_psalm row was rejected: web:Ps.101.5 turns from the psalmist's own conduct to action taken against others, an addressee-object shift strong enough to seam the psalm at 101:4|101:5.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: אַשְׂכִּ֤ילָה בְּדֶ֬רֶךְ תָּמִ֗ים (oshb:Ps.101.2) opens the psalm's personal-resolve section with a first-person cohortative, matching the register of web:Ps.101.1's opening vow.

rationale: The strophe turns from the psalmist's own heart to conduct among others: web:Ps.101.5 opens “I will silence whoever secretly slanders his neighbor.” (byte: מלושני מְלָשְׁנִ֬י, oshb:Ps.101.5), naming those who will not dwell in his house through web:Ps.101.6-101.7 (“He who practices deceit won’t dwell within my house.”), and closes on the purge clause of web:Ps.101.8, “Morning by morning, I will destroy all the wicked of the land” (byte: לַבְּקָרִ֗ים אַצְמִ֥ית כָּל רִשְׁעֵי אָ֑רֶץ, oshb:Ps.101.8).
rejected_alternative: Treating 101:5 as the opening of a new psalm-level unit rather than a strophe within Psalm 101 was rejected: the parent grouping stated at this psalm's opening row still governs every row of Psalm 101.
observed_substrate_signals: byte: מלושני מְלָשְׁנִ֬י (oshb:Ps.101.5) straddles a ketiv/qere spelling pair, the defective ketiv spelling set beside the pointed qere spelling — disclosed per the kq inventory (pmarks_Ps.json); both spellings are the same word, plene against defective.

rationale: The psalm opens on its superscription, “A Prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed and pours out his complaint before Yahweh.” (web:Ps.102.0), a tefillah (תְּ֭פִלָּה, oshb:Ps.102.1) title naming a genre rather than a person — tier-1 opener evidence. The double imperative plea that follows, “Hear my prayer, Yahweh! Let my cry come to you.” (web:Ps.102.1) and “Don’t hide your face from me in the day of my distress. Turn your ear to me. Answer me quickly in the day when I call.” (web:Ps.102.2), addresses Yahweh directly in the second person, and the reason-clause “For my days consume away like smoke. My bones are burned as a torch.” (web:Ps.102.3) closes the invocation just before the grass-bracketed complaint body opens at web:Ps.102.4.
rejected_alternative: Folding the whole individual-lament movement into one row was rejected because the grass inclusio marks a tighter unit that begins at web:Ps.102.4, leaving the vocative-imperative opening and its reason-clause (web:Ps.102.1-Ps.102.3) as the invocation proper.
observed_substrate_signals: title tefillah label תְּ֭פִלָּה (oshb:Ps.102.1) carries no name attribution, unlike the historical-note titles elsewhere in the book
the row's imperative plea (web:Ps.102.1-Ps.102.2) addresses Yahweh in the second person, matching the psalm's title framing of a sufferer's direct complaint
device_notes: These rows resolve upward to Psalm 102 as parent. The tefillah title (web:Ps.102.0) and the psalm's own three-part movement — individual lament, Zion-restoration, and creation-permanence — shape the rows that follow.

rationale: This span is bracketed by the same simile word: “My heart is blighted like grass, and withered, for I forget to eat my bread.” (web:Ps.102.4) opens with כָ֭עֵשֶׂב (oshb:Ps.102.5), and “My days are like a long shadow. I have withered like grass.” (web:Ps.102.11) closes with כָּעֵ֥שֶׂב (oshb:Ps.102.12) — the same lexeme עשב bracketing the complaint body, skeleton-matching across the 2 verses (oshb:Ps.102.5, oshb:Ps.102.12). Between the brackets the row moves from bodily affliction (“By reason of the voice of my groaning, my bones stick to my skin.”, web:Ps.102.5) through the paired bird similes (“I am like a pelican of the wilderness. I have become as an owl of the waste places.”, web:Ps.102.6, and “I watch, and have become like a sparrow that is alone on the housetop.”, web:Ps.102.7) to the enemies' reproach (“My enemies reproach me all day. Those who are mad at me use my name as a curse.”, web:Ps.102.8), the ashes-for-bread image (web:Ps.102.9), and the second-person address returning at “because of your indignation and your wrath; for you have taken me up and thrown me away.” (web:Ps.102.10) before the shadow-and-grass close at web:Ps.102.11.
rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at the pelican/owl/sparrow simile pair (web:Ps.102.6-web:Ps.102.7) into two shorter rows was rejected because it would cut the grass-bracketed unit without any comparable seam signal inside it.
observed_substrate_signals: כָ֭עֵשֶׂב (web:Ps.102.4 = oshb:Ps.102.5) and כָּעֵ֥שֶׂב (web:Ps.102.11 = oshb:Ps.102.12) share the consonantal root עשב, bracketing the span
second-person address is absent across web:Ps.102.3-web:Ps.102.9 (seven verses) and returns at web:Ps.102.10, inside this row's own close
device_notes: This row is the individual-lament movement's body, framed by the grass inclusio (web:Ps.102.4, web:Ps.102.11) inside one row rather than split across the seam.

rationale: The row opens on the tier-1 adversative and addressee pivot, “But you, Yahweh, will remain forever; your renown endures to all generations.” (web:Ps.102.12), whose Hebrew opens וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.102.13) — a conjunctive vav plus the independent second-person pronoun אתה that readdresses Yahweh directly in the second person after web:Ps.102.3-web:Ps.102.9 (seven verses) run without it, the address returning briefly at web:Ps.102.10 before this row's own return at web:Ps.102.12. The turn opens the Zion oracle: “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is time to have pity on her. Yes, the set time has come.” (web:Ps.102.13), the servants' pleasure “For your servants take pleasure in her stones, and have pity on her dust.” (web:Ps.102.14), the nations' fear of Yahweh's name (web:Ps.102.15), and the report “For Yahweh has built up Zion. He has appeared in his glory.” (web:Ps.102.16), which closes the row on a completed-action note.
rejected_alternative: Extending the row through web:Ps.102.22 as one continuous Zion-oracle block was rejected because web:Ps.102.16's completed-action report closes the arise-and-rebuild movement before web:Ps.102.17 opens a new causal chain.
observed_substrate_signals: וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה (web:Ps.102.12 = oshb:Ps.102.13) pairs the conjunctive vav with the independent pronoun אתה, a stronger contrastive marking than a bare vav
device_notes: The Zion-restoration movement (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) begins here; this row covers its rebuilding half.

rationale: The row opens on a new causal chain, “He has responded to the prayer of the destitute, and has not despised their prayer.” (web:Ps.102.17), pivoting from the completed rebuilding report that closes the previous row (web:Ps.102.16) to a forward-looking purpose clause, “This will be written for the generation to come. A people which will be created will praise Yah,” (web:Ps.102.18); the sanctuary vantage “for he has looked down from the height of his sanctuary. From heaven, Yahweh saw the earth,” (web:Ps.102.19) opens onto the prisoner's release (web:Ps.102.20) and the proclamation “that men may declare Yahweh’s name in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem,” (web:Ps.102.21), closing on “when the peoples are gathered together, the kingdoms, to serve Yahweh.” (web:Ps.102.22).
rejected_alternative: Grouping web:Ps.102.17 with the preceding rebuilding report (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.16) was rejected because the purpose clause at web:Ps.102.18 opens a distinct forward-looking movement that this row keeps intact through its close at web:Ps.102.22.
observed_substrate_signals: the purpose clause at web:Ps.102.18 ('this will be written for the generation to come') marks a future-oriented register shift from the completed-action report closing web:Ps.102.16
device_notes: This row completes the Zion-restoration movement opened at web:Ps.102.12, closing on the nations gathered to serve Yahweh before web:Ps.102.23 returns to the psalmist's own voice.

rationale: The row returns abruptly to the psalmist's own voice, “He weakened my strength along the course. He shortened my days.” (web:Ps.102.23), reopening the first-person complaint that closed at web:Ps.102.11 and that the intervening Zion oracle (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) had set aside; MT web:Ps.102.23 (oshb:Ps.102.24) carries a ketiv כחו against a qere כֹּחִ֗י (pmarks_Ps.json kq), disclosed here though this row's boundary does not depend on either reading. The direct petition “I said, “My God, don’t take me away in the middle of my days. Your years are throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.102.24) turns at web:Ps.102.25 to creation theology, “Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands.” (לְ֭פָנִים הָאָ֣רֶץ יָסַ֑דְתָּ, oshb:Ps.102.26), and closes on the contrast between what perishes and what endures, “They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed.” (web:Ps.102.26), “But you are the same. Your years will have no end.” (web:Ps.102.27), and the hope “The children of your servants will continue. Their offspring will be established before you.”” (web:Ps.102.28).
rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.102.23-web:Ps.102.24 as a continuation of the Zion oracle was rejected because the first-person pronouns reopen the psalmist's own complaint voice that the third-person Zion report (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) had set aside.
observed_substrate_signals: MT oshb:Ps.102.24 carries a ketiv/qere pair כחו כֹּחִ֗י inside this row's span (web:Ps.102.23), matching pmarks_Ps.json's kq entry for this verse
device_notes: This row closes Psalm 102, moving from the psalmist's shortened days (web:Ps.102.23) through the earth's foundation (web:Ps.102.25) to the enduring servants' line (web:Ps.102.28).

rationale: The title “By David.” (web:Ps.103.0) sits as the prefix לְדָוִ֨ד of MT v.1 (oshb:Ps.103.1) rather than a separate counted verse — an identity-psalm title, still tier-1 opener evidence. The psalm opens on the self-summons “Praise Yahweh, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!” (web:Ps.103.1), whose Hebrew clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1) the psalm's own close will echo; “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,” (web:Ps.103.2) turns the summons into a catalog, itemized across “who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,” (web:Ps.103.3), “who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies,” (web:Ps.103.4), as well as “who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” (web:Ps.103.5), continuing the second-person address to the summoned soul.
rejected_alternative: Starting the row at web:Ps.103.2 and treating web:Ps.103.1 as title-adjacent overflow was rejected because the barchi-nafshi clause already appears in web:Ps.103.1 itself, not merely in the title.
observed_substrate_signals: the title word לְדָוִ֨ד (oshb:Ps.103.1) sits inside MT v.1 with no separate title verse number, matching the identity-psalm numbering rule
device_notes: The parent unit here is the full Psalm 103. Its opening and closing clauses (web:Ps.103.1, web:Ps.103.22) form the barchi-nafshi inclusio that frames the whole psalm; this row carries the inclusio's opening half.

rationale: The row's grammatical subject shifts from the summoned soul to Yahweh himself: “Yahweh executes righteous acts, and justice for all who are oppressed.” (web:Ps.103.6) opens with the participle עֹשֵׂ֣ה צְדָק֣וֹת (oshb:Ps.103.6), moving from second-person imperative address (web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5) to third-person declaration; “He made known his ways to Moses, his deeds to the children of Israel.” (web:Ps.103.7) grounds the declaration historically before the row states Yahweh's own character, “Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.” (web:Ps.103.8), and closes on the negated-accusation pair “He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.” (web:Ps.103.9) and “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” (web:Ps.103.10).
rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.103.6 with the preceding catalog (web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5) was rejected because the shift from second-person imperative address to third-person declaration about Yahweh marks a distinct discourse register.
observed_substrate_signals: עֹשֵׂ֣ה צְדָק֣וֹת (oshb:Ps.103.6) is a participial third-person predicate, unlike the second-person imperative clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1) opening the row before it
device_notes: This row opens the chesed catalog's declarative half, restating in the third person what the second-person summons of web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5 addressed to the soul.

rationale: A chain of comparative similes opens the row, “For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.” (web:Ps.103.11), Hebrew כִּ֤י כִגְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם (oshb:Ps.103.11) — a comparison construction the declarative catalog of web:Ps.103.6-web:Ps.103.10 does not use; “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” (web:Ps.103.12) and “Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.” (web:Ps.103.13) continue the pattern before the row turns from simile to cause, “For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” (web:Ps.103.14), Hebrew כִּי עָפָ֥ר אֲנָֽחְנוּ (oshb:Ps.103.14) — the dust motif that hinges into the transience movement of web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16.
rejected_alternative: Placing web:Ps.103.14 with the transience movement that follows (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16) was rejected because its verb still has Yahweh as subject, matching the compassion-simile chain rather than the new grammatical subject, man, that opens web:Ps.103.15.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּ֤י כִגְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם (oshb:Ps.103.11) opens with the comparison particle כי, repeated in כִּי עָפָ֥ר אֲנָֽחְנוּ (oshb:Ps.103.14) as a plain causal use rather than a fresh simile
device_notes: The dust motif closing this row (web:Ps.103.14) hinges toward the grass-and-flower transience imagery of the next row without changing grammatical subject.

rationale: The subject changes to man at the row's opening, “As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes.” (web:Ps.103.15), continued by the wind image “For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.” (web:Ps.103.16); the vav-initial clause “But Yahweh’s loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting with those who fear him, his righteousness to children’s children,” (web:Ps.103.17), Hebrew וְחֶ֤סֶד יְהוָ֨ה (oshb:Ps.103.17) — a plainer conjunctive-vav contrast than the emphatic pronoun-plus-vav pivot at web:Ps.102.12, but still legible against the transience just described — pivots back to Yahweh as subject and closes the row on the covenant-keepers of “to those who keep his covenant, to those who remember to obey his precepts.” (web:Ps.103.18).
rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.103.17's vav-clause as a return to the preceding compassion-simile row (web:Ps.103.11-web:Ps.103.14) was rejected because it answers the intervening transience description (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16), not the simile chain three verses earlier.
observed_substrate_signals: וְחֶ֤סֶד יְהוָ֨ה (oshb:Ps.103.17) opens with a plain conjunctive vav on חסד, weaker than the vav-plus-pronoun construction וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה at oshb:Ps.102.13
device_notes: This row's transience-to-chesed pivot (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.17) parallels in shape, though not in Hebrew grammatical force, the adversative turn at web:Ps.102.12 elsewhere in this part.

rationale: The row opens on the enthronement declaration “Yahweh has established his throne in the heavens. His kingdom rules over all.” (web:Ps.103.19), Hebrew יְֽהוָ֗ה בַּ֭שָּׁמַיִם הֵכִ֣ין (oshb:Ps.103.19), then widens the imperative ‘praise Yahweh’ from the soul addressed at web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.2 outward to the angels, “Praise Yahweh, you angels of his, who are mighty in strength, who fulfill his word, obeying the voice of his word.” (web:Ps.103.20), Hebrew בָּרֲכ֥וּ יְהוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.103.20) — a plural imperative, unlike the singular בָּרֲכִ֣י (oshb:Ps.103.1) addressed to the soul — then to his armies and his works (web:Ps.103.21-web:Ps.103.22) before the row's own closing clause, “Praise Yahweh, all you works of his, in all places of his dominion. Praise Yahweh, my soul!” (web:Ps.103.22), returns to the singular imperative and to the clause the psalm opened with. That closing clause, Hebrew בָּרֲכִ֥י נַ֝פְשִׁ֗י אֶת יְהוָֽה (oshb:Ps.103.22), is skeleton-identical, across the 2 verses (oshb:Ps.103.1, oshb:Ps.103.22), to the opening clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1); the two differ only in the trailing accent mark on the final word, an expected verse-final cantillation difference rather than a textual variant, so the match is claimed at the skeleton tier, not the byte tier.
rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.103.22 as belonging with the cosmic-praise catalog of web:Ps.103.20-web:Ps.103.21 without separately flagging its closing clause was rejected because that clause repeats the psalm's own opening words and closes the inclusio opened at web:Ps.103.1.
observed_substrate_signals: בָּרֲכ֥וּ יְהוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.103.20) is a plural imperative addressed to the angels, contrasting with the singular בָּרֲכִ֣י (oshb:Ps.103.1, oshb:Ps.103.22) addressed to the soul
the closing clause (oshb:Ps.103.22) matches the opening clause (oshb:Ps.103.1) at the skeleton tier across the 2 verses; only the final word's cantillation mark differs
device_notes: This row closes the barchi-nafshi inclusio opened at web:Ps.103.1, completing Psalm 103's parent grouping; the angelic call-to-bless (web:Ps.103.20-web:Ps.103.21) widens the summons before the closing return to my soul.

rationale: The psalm opens with the imperative inclusio that frames it, “Bless Yahweh, my soul” (web:Ps.104.1), with the Hebrew 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' at oshb:Ps.104.1; the address then turns to second-person praise of Yahweh’s robing in light before shifting to third-person description of the heavens stretched “like a curtain” (web:Ps.104.2), the waters-roofed chambers and cloud-chariot (web:Ps.104.3), and the wind/fire messengers (web:Ps.104.4). This four-verse unit covers the robing-in-light and sky-building movement before the earth itself becomes the subject at 104:5.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 104:5 (the earth’s foundation) was considered, but 104:5 introduces a new created object (the earth, not the heavens) under a new governing verb, marking a fresh movement rather than a continuation of the sky-building imagery.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative inclusio opener 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1, tier: byte)
movement covers robing/light, heavens-as-curtain, water-chambers, cloud-chariot, wind/fire messengers (104:2-4)
the governing subject shifts from the heavens (104:2-4) to the earth (104:5), tier-1 topic seam
device_notes: Psalm 104 stands as one liturgical composition; every row below shares its single parent, Psalm 104. The opening 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1) recurs verbatim at the psalm’s own close (oshb:Ps.104.35) as its inclusio; the identical phrase also frames the preceding psalm as its own opener and closer — sweep: 5 verses book-wide carry the skeleton 'ברכי נפשי', three of them outside this psalm — a typed cross-psalm relation (shared inclusio phrasing), never a merged row or shared authorship claim.

rationale: A new creative act opens the unit: “He laid the foundations of the earth” (web:Ps.104.5) — the Hebrew reads 'יָֽסַד אֶ֭רֶץ' (oshb:Ps.104.5) — governed by the verb 'יָֽסַד' (roughly 'founded') rather than the stretching/covering verbs of 104:2-4. The unit then narrates the primeval waters standing above the mountains (web:Ps.104.6), fleeing “At your rebuke” and “the voice of your thunder” (web:Ps.104.7), the mountains rising and valleys sinking (web:Ps.104.8), and closes on the fixed boundary set so the waters “may not pass over” and “don't turn again to cover the earth” (web:Ps.104.9).
rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 104:8 and folding the boundary clause (104:9) into the following springs unit was considered, but 104:9’s “that they may not pass over” completes the waters-in-retreat action begun at 104:6-7, not the springs-in-the-valleys topic that opens fresh at 104:10.
observed_substrate_signals: governing verb shifts from participial sky-building (104:2-4) to perfect 'יָֽסַד' 'founded' (104:5, oshb:Ps.104.5), tier-2 topic seam
second-person address to the primeval waters runs 104:6-9 as one action sequence (flee, retreat, boundary-set)

rationale: The topic turns from the sea’s retreat to fresh water given: “He sends springs into the valleys” (web:Ps.104.10), matching 'הַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֣חַ מַ֭עְיָנִים' at oshb:Ps.104.10, a new participial verb ('הַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֣חַ', roughly 'the one who sends') opening a distinct movement. Animals drink at these springs (web:Ps.104.11), birds nest and sing by them (web:Ps.104.12), and the unit closes with Yahweh watering the mountains “from his rooms” so “The earth is filled with the fruit of your works” (web:Ps.104.13).
rejected_alternative: Running 104:10-13 together with the vegetation catalogue of 104:14-18 as one long unit was considered, but 104:14 opens with its own new participial verb ('מַצְמִ֤יחַ', roughly 'causing to sprout,' oshb:Ps.104.14) governing plant growth, a distinct topic from the springs/mountain-watering of 104:10-13.
observed_substrate_signals: new participial verb 'הַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֣חַ' opens the unit (104:10, oshb:Ps.104.10), tier-2 topic seam
unit runs springs → animal drink → bird nesting → mountain-watering as one water-provision sequence

rationale: A second participial verb opens a new movement: “He causes the grass to grow” (web:Ps.104.14), whose Hebrew is 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ חָצִ֨יר' (oshb:Ps.104.14), governing vegetation rather than water. The catalogue runs through wine, oil, and bread “that strengthens man's heart” (web:Ps.104.15), the well-watered cedars of Lebanon “which he has planted” (web:Ps.104.16), nesting birds and the stork’s home in the cypress trees (web:Ps.104.17), and closes with the high mountains for wild goats and the rocks as “a refuge for the rock badgers” (web:Ps.104.18).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the human provisions (104:14-15) from the tree/animal habitat material (104:16-18) as two rows was considered, but both develop the same 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ' (oshb:Ps.104.14)-governed vegetation catalogue with no addressee or verb-class break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: new participial verb 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ' opens the unit (104:14, oshb:Ps.104.14), tier-2 topic seam
catalogue moves from cultivated food (14-15) to wild trees and their animal residents (16-18) within one vegetation topic

rationale: The topic turns to the luminaries: “He appointed the moon for seasons” (web:Ps.104.19), rendering 'עָשָׂ֣ה יָ֭רֵחַ לְמוֹעֲדִ֑ים' (oshb:Ps.104.19), a perfect verb ('עָשָׂ֣ה', roughly 'he made') that opens the day/night movement. Darkness and the forest’s prowling animals follow (web:Ps.104.20), young lions roaring for prey “from God” (web:Ps.104.21), the sun’s rising and the lions’ retreat to their dens (web:Ps.104.22), and the unit closes on man going out “to his labor until the evening” (web:Ps.104.23), completing the diurnal cycle the moon and sun opened.
rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 104:22 (the lions’ retreat) and giving man’s labor its own one-verse row was considered, but 104:23 completes the same night-to-day handoff opened at 104:20 rather than starting an independent topic.
observed_substrate_signals: new perfect verb 'עָשָׂ֣ה' opens the luminaries topic (104:19, oshb:Ps.104.19), tier-2 topic seam
unit alternates night (20-21) and day (22-23) actors around the sun/moon appointment, one diurnal-cycle movement

rationale: A wisdom-exclamation in direct address opens the unit, breaking the third-person description that dominates the surrounding verses: “Yahweh, how many are your works!” (web:Ps.104.24), collated to 'מָֽה רַבּ֬וּ מַעֲשֶׂ֨יךָ יְֽהוָ֗ה' (oshb:Ps.104.24). “The earth is full of your riches” leads into the sea catalogue: “There is the sea, great and wide” (web:Ps.104.25), with ships and “leviathan, whom you formed to play there” (web:Ps.104.26), set against 'לִ֝וְיָתָ֗ן' (oshb:Ps.104.26).
rejected_alternative: Running 104:24-30 together as one providence unit was considered, but 104:27 opens with the collective pronoun 'כֻּ֭לָּם' (roughly 'the whole of them,' oshb:Ps.104.27) turning the address from the sea’s specific inhabitants to creation’s general dependence, a distinct referential class from the sea catalogue of 104:24-26.
observed_substrate_signals: direct-address wisdom exclamation opens the unit (104:24), a mode shift from the surrounding third-person description
sea catalogue (104:25-26) is a self-contained topic bounded by the exclamation before it and the collective-pronoun pickup after it
device_notes: WEB renders the sea creature at 104:26 as lowercase “leviathan” (byte-tier reading of the clean WEB text, not a title or proper-name capitalization); sweep: 2 verses book-wide carry the skeleton 'לויתן' (oshb:Ps.104.26), one other occurrence sitting outside this psalm.

rationale: The collective pronoun opens a new address class: “These all wait for you” (web:Ps.104.27) — MT reads 'כֻּ֭לָּם אֵלֶ֣יךָ יְשַׂבֵּר֑וּן' (oshb:Ps.104.27) — turning from the sea’s named inhabitants to creation’s general dependence, run through a sustained second-person cluster: “You give… You open your hand” (web:Ps.104.28), “You hide your face… You take away their breath” (web:Ps.104.29), plus “You send out your Spirit… You renew the face of the ground” (web:Ps.104.30), which closes the providence movement before the doxological response opens at 104:31.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 104:31 was considered, but 104:31 shifts to jussive mode ('יְהִ֤י', roughly 'let there be,' oshb:Ps.104.31) petitioning on Yahweh’s behalf, a distinct grammatical mood from the second-person description of divine action in 104:27-30.
observed_substrate_signals: collective pronoun 'כֻּ֭לָּם' opens the unit (104:27, oshb:Ps.104.27), addressee-class shift from named sea creatures to creation broadly
sustained 2nd-person give/open/hide/take/send/renew verb cluster runs 104:28-30 as one providence-and-mortality sequence

rationale: The mode shifts to jussive petition: “Let Yahweh's glory endure forever” (web:Ps.104.31), the Hebrew 'יְהִ֤י כְב֣וֹד יְהוָ֣ה לְעוֹלָ֑ם' at oshb:Ps.104.31, a grammatical break from the second-person description preceding it. Third-person description of Yahweh’s power returns at 104:32, then the psalmist’s own first-person vow opens at “I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live” (web:Ps.104.33); the Hebrew 'אָשִׁ֣ירָה' underlies it at oshb:Ps.104.33, and continues through 104:34, before the unit closes with a wish against sinners, the psalm’s own inclusio — “Bless Yahweh, my soul” (web:Ps.104.35), in Hebrew 'בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי' (oshb:Ps.104.35) — and the hallelu-Yah that ends the psalm: 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.104.35).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the closing doxology (104:31-32) from the first-person vow and final wish (104:33-35) as two rows was considered, but no selah or addressee-class break separates them, and the inclusio at 104:35 answers the imperative that opened the whole psalm at 104:1, tying the closing movement together as one unit.
observed_substrate_signals: jussive mode 'יְהִ֤י' opens the doxological turn (104:31, oshb:Ps.104.31), grammatical mood shift from the preceding second-person providence cluster
first-person vow ('אָשִׁ֣ירָה', oshb:Ps.104.33) opens at 104:33, a further register shift within the same unit
inclusio 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1) closes the unit as a byte-tier repeat of 104:1 (2 occurrences within this psalm), then hallelu-Yah closes the psalm verse-finally
device_notes: Psalm 104 closes with 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.104.35), the earliest by psalm order among the curated hallelu-Yah frame inventory’s 25 book-wide occurrences (psalm_device_inventory.json: sweep: 11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final + 1 interior = 25); a naive skeleton substring sweep for 'הללו יה' returns 26 hits because it also matches the imperfect verb “yehalelu” (“they will praise”) run directly into the start of the divine name at oshb:Ps.22.27 — a consonantal false positive, not a hallelu-Yah particle; the curated inventory, not the naive sweep, is the count of record. As texture: hallelu-Yah also opens and closes the two following psalms in this cluster, not evidence bearing on this row's own close.

rationale: The psalm opens with the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH call: “Give thanks to Yahweh!” (web:Ps.105.1), with the Hebrew 'הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה' at oshb:Ps.105.1, a tier-1 opener device (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings). The imperative cluster continues: “Call on his name” (web:Ps.105.1), “Sing to him, sing praises to him” (web:Ps.105.2), “Glory in his holy name” (web:Ps.105.3), “Seek Yahweh and his strength” (web:Ps.105.4), and also “Remember his marvelous works” (web:Ps.105.5), before the unit closes addressing “you offspring of Abraham… you children of Jacob, his chosen ones” (web:Ps.105.6), naming the addressees the historical recital that follows will retell.
rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:5 (its final imperative) and giving the vocative “offspring of Abraham” its own row was considered, but 105:6 is the grammatical object of 105:5’s “remember,” not an independent clause, so splitting it would sever the imperative from its addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH opener ('הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה', 105:1, oshb:Ps.105.1), tier-1 device per the frame inventory
sustained imperative-cluster mode runs 105:1-6 (give thanks, call, sing, glory, seek, remember), closing on the vocative addressee it governs
device_notes: Psalm 105 coheres as one composition — parent grouping Psalm 105; every row below shares that single parent. The historical recital moves covenant → Joseph → Egypt/plagues → exodus → settlement across the rows that follow.

rationale: A declarative statement opens the unit with its own independent pronoun: “He is Yahweh, our God” (web:Ps.105.7) — the Hebrew reads 'ה֭וּא יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ' (oshb:Ps.105.7) — turning from the imperative calls of 105:1-6 to covenant declaration. “He has remembered his covenant forever” (web:Ps.105.8) names “the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac” (web:Ps.105.9), matching 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' at oshb:Ps.105.9, confirmed “to Jacob… to Israel” (web:Ps.105.10), and closes with the land grant quoted in direct speech: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance” (web:Ps.105.11).
rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:10 and giving the quoted land grant (105:11) its own row was considered, but 105:11’s “saying” clause is the direct object of 105:8-10’s covenant-remembering, not a new speech act beginning a fresh unit.
observed_substrate_signals: independent-pronoun declaration 'ה֭וּא' opens the unit (105:7, oshb:Ps.105.7), a subject-class shift from the imperative mode of 105:1-6
covenant chain runs patriarch-by-patriarch (Abraham 105:9, Jacob/Israel 105:10) to its quoted land-grant close (105:11)
device_notes: The oath “to Isaac” at 105:9 is spelled 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' (oshb:Ps.105.9) with sin rather than the standard tzade; a skeleton sweep for the sin-spelling 'לישחק' returns 4 verses book-wide, but only 105:9 is the proper name — the other three are the common verb “he will laugh” (root s-h-q), a consonantal homograph found elsewhere in the Psalter; a skeleton sweep for the standard tzade spelling returns 0 verses book-wide, so 105:9 is the Psalter’s one occurrence of Isaac’s name, and it carries the alternate spelling.

rationale: A temporal clause opens the narrative proper: “when they were but a few men in number” (web:Ps.105.12), whose Hebrew is 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם מְתֵ֣י מִסְפָּ֑ר' (oshb:Ps.105.12), shifting from covenant declaration to the patriarchs’ own wandering. “They went about from nation to nation” (web:Ps.105.13) and Yahweh “reproved kings for their sakes” (web:Ps.105.14), closing on the quoted royal warning: “Don't touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!” (web:Ps.105.15), rendering 'אַֽל תִּגְּע֥וּ בִמְשִׁיחָ֑י' (oshb:Ps.105.15).
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 105:16 was considered, but 105:16 opens with a wayyiqtol narrative verb ('וַיִּקְרָ֣א', roughly 'and he called,' oshb:Ps.105.16) beginning the famine that triggers the Joseph narrative, a new narrative-sequence link rather than a continuation of the royal-protection material.
observed_substrate_signals: temporal clause 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם' opens the unit (105:12, oshb:Ps.105.12), a narrative-time shift into the patriarchal period
unit closes on quoted divine speech protecting “my anointed ones” / “my prophets” (105:15)

rationale: A wayyiqtol narrative verb opens the Joseph story: “He called for a famine on the land” (web:Ps.105.16), collated to 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א רָ֭עָב' (oshb:Ps.105.16). “He sent a man before them. Joseph was sold for a slave” (web:Ps.105.17), set against 'יוֹסֵֽף' (oshb:Ps.105.17), his feet bruised “with shackles” (web:Ps.105.18) until “Yahweh's word proved him true” (web:Ps.105.19), the king’s release of him (web:Ps.105.20), his rule over the royal house (web:Ps.105.21), and the unit closes with Joseph’s authority “to discipline his princes… and to teach his elders wisdom” (web:Ps.105.22).
rejected_alternative: Splitting Joseph’s imprisonment (105:17-19) from his exaltation (105:20-22) as two rows was considered, but both develop one reversal-of-fortune narrative arc without a named-subject change or narrative-time break between them; the arc runs to its close at 105:22 before Israel corporately enters at 105:23.
observed_substrate_signals: wayyiqtol narrative verb 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א' opens the unit (105:16, oshb:Ps.105.16), narrative-sequence link distinct from the temporal clause of 105:12
one named subject (Joseph) governs the whole unit from sale (105:17) through the household he comes to rule (105:20-22)
device_notes: A ketiv/qere note sits at oshb:Ps.105.18 (pmarks_Ps.json kq) on the word rendered “his feet”/“his foot”; not quoted here, disclosed because the span crosses it.

rationale: A new wayyiqtol verb introduces a new named subject: “Israel also came into Egypt” (web:Ps.105.23) — MT reads 'וַיָּבֹ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מִצְרָ֑יִם' (oshb:Ps.105.23) — turning from Joseph individually to Israel corporately. “He increased his people greatly” (web:Ps.105.24) and “turned their heart to hate his people” (web:Ps.105.25) set up the oppression that “He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron” answers (web:Ps.105.26), the Hebrew 'שָׁ֭לַח מֹשֶׁ֣ה עַבְדּ֑וֹ' at oshb:Ps.105.26; the unit closes with Moses and Aaron performing “miracles among them, and wonders in the land of Ham” (web:Ps.105.27), the general statement the plague catalogue itemizes from 105:28.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through the whole nine-verse plague list was considered, but 105:28 opens the itemized catalogue proper with its own perfect verb ('שָׁ֣לַֽח', roughly 'he sent [darkness],' oshb:Ps.105.28), where 105:27 still speaks in the general terms (“miracles… wonders”) that the catalogue then specifies.
observed_substrate_signals: new wayyiqtol verb with new named subject Israel opens the unit (105:23), narrative-subject shift from Joseph
unit runs population growth → oppression → the sending of Moses/Aaron → a general miracles/wonders statement that the following catalogue itemizes
device_notes: The plague sequence itemized from 105:28 (darkness, blood, frogs, insects, hail, locusts, and the death of the “firstborn”) covers 7 of the traditional plagues and omits the livestock-pestilence and boils material present in this psalm's own catalogue by their absence; a cross-book relation to Exodus’s narrative noted as texture, not boundary authority for these rows.

rationale: The plague catalogue opens: “He sent darkness, and made it dark” (web:Ps.105.28); the Hebrew 'שָׁ֣לַֽח חֹ֭שֶׁךְ' underlies it at oshb:Ps.105.28, opening a four-plague disruption group: waters “turned… into blood” killing the fish (web:Ps.105.29), the land “swarmed with frogs, even in the rooms of their kings” (web:Ps.105.30), and “swarms of flies… and lice in all their borders” (web:Ps.105.31), which closes the group before the destruction-class plagues open at 105:32.
