rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 132:13, where Zion's election is initially named, was considered; rejected because 132:13 is third-person narration while 132:14 is the oracle's own first-person voice, marked by the WEB quotation boundary.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person divine quotation opens web:Ps.132.14 and closes at the psalm's own end, web:Ps.132.18 (WEB quotation marks)
no selah in Ps.132.14-Ps.132.18 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

rationale: Unlike 132, Psalm 133's title carries a name in title position: “שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד” (oshb:Ps.133.1) (oshb:Ps.133.1) places the David-word directly after the genre label, a le-David attribution -- contrast 132:1 (web:Ps.132.0 = oshb:Ps.132.1), where the same word functions as the verb's indirect object, not a title element. Its three verses move as one indivisible image: “הִנֵּ֣ה מַה טּ֭וֹב וּמַה נָּעִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.133.1) -- “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (web:Ps.133.1) -- develops through the anointing-oil simile (web:Ps.133.2) into the dew-of-Hermon simile and its closing blessing, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (web:Ps.133.3). No vocative, quotation, or addressee shift divides the three verses; the whole is one wisdom-styled beatitude on communal unity.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the oil simile (133:2) from the dew simile (133:3) was considered, since the two develop distinct images; rejected as the two similes share one grammatical frame (comparison clauses elaborating 133:1's opening exclamation) with no independent seam marker between them.
observed_substrate_signals: title (oshb:Ps.133.1): “שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד” -- the David-word sits in title position, immediately after the genre label (contrast 132:1)
psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions entry for 133 lists le_david alongside shir/shir_hammaalot
no selah in Ps.133 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence, whole psalm)
device_notes: Psalm 133 anchors the parent grouping for these rows. -- Psalm 133 entire.

rationale: Psalm 134's title repeats 132's own wording, bare shir hamma'alot with no name attached (web:Ps.134.0 = oshb:Ps.134.1). Its three verses form one antiphonal exchange: an imperative call to the night-watch temple servants, “Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house!” (web:Ps.134.1), continuing “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.134.2), then a reply that reverses the direction of blessing: “יְבָרֶכְךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה מִצִּיּ֑וֹן” (oshb:Ps.134.3) -- “May Yahweh bless you from Zion, even he who made heaven and earth.” (web:Ps.134.3). The call (134:1-2) addresses the servants in the imperative; the reply (134:3) turns the blessing back onto whoever has just spoken it, closing the short ascents collection's coda with this exchange rather than a further imperative.
rejected_alternative: Treating 134:1-2 and 134:3 as two rows was considered, since the addressee reverses between them (servants addressed, then the worshipper blessed); rejected under the owner ruling for short indivisible psalms (roughly <=8 verses) -- three verses is too little to divide without padding.
observed_substrate_signals: title: shir hamma'alot, no name label (as 132, against 133's le-David; oshb:Ps.134.1)
second-person imperative addressee ("you" plural, the servants) in 134:1-2 reverses to second-person singular blessing-recipient in 134:3
no selah in Ps.134 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence, whole psalm)
device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition: parent grouping Psalm 134, whole and undivided.

rationale: Untitled, Psalm 135 opens “הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַֽ֭לְלוּ אֶת שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.1) -- “Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh's name! Praise him, you servants of Yahweh,” (web:Ps.135.1) -- an imperative call to praise that continues through web:Ps.135.3's own hallelu-Yah (‘Praise Yah, for Yahweh is good. Sing praises to his name, for that is pleasant.’), then supplies an opening motive for praise, “For Yah has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.” (web:Ps.135.4). The psalm's hallelu-Yah frame opens here in both its occurrences (verse-initial at 135:1 and 135:3, per psalm_device_inventory.json's halleluyah inventory) and, on that inventory, recurs verse-finally at the psalm's own close -- a frame this opening row does not itself carry evidence for past its own span.
rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 135:3, keeping just the imperative praise-calls together, was considered and is a serious rival reading; 135:4 is kept with it because both 135:4 and 135:5's motive clauses open with the same particle ("for"), so the seam more clearly marked by content sits at 135:4|5, not 135:3|4.
observed_substrate_signals: hallelu-Yah verse-initial at web:Ps.135.1 and web:Ps.135.3 (psalm_device_inventory.json halleluyah.verse_initial; 2 of the book's 11 verse-initial occurrences fall in this span)
motive-clause particle "for" opens both 135:4 and the following verse 135:5, a lexical bridge across this row's own closing seam
device_notes: One parent, Psalm 135, spans every row below it.

rationale: “כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי כִּי גָד֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.5) -- “For I know that Yahweh is great, that our Lord is above all gods.” (web:Ps.135.5) -- opens a declarative unit that runs through creation (“Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth,” web:Ps.135.6; the clouds, lightning, and wind of web:Ps.135.7) into historical recital: “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and animal.” (web:Ps.135.8), signs and wonders sent on Pharaoh (web:Ps.135.9), many nations and mighty kings struck (web:Ps.135.10), “Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan-” (web:Ps.135.11), and their land given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.135.12). Every verse (8 of 8, 135:5-12) stays in the third person describing Yahweh's own acts; the row closes where that third-person description turns to direct second-person address at web:Ps.135.13 (“Your name, Yahweh, endures forever”).
rejected_alternative: Splitting creation (135:5-7) from the historical recital (135:8-12) was considered; rejected because no vocative, quotation, or addressee change marks that content transition -- both remain third-person description under 135:5's own governing clause.
observed_substrate_signals: third-person description of Yahweh's acts runs unbroken from web:Ps.135.5 through web:Ps.135.12
second-person address ("your name", "your renown") opens immediately after this row's own close, at web:Ps.135.13

rationale: “יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְךָ֣ לְעוֹלָ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.135.13) -- “Your name, Yahweh, endures forever; your renown, Yahweh, throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.135.13) -- turns briefly to direct second-person address of Yahweh, naming him twice by vocative; web:Ps.135.14 then reverts to third person, “For Yahweh will judge his people and have compassion on his servants.” This two-verse span sits as a hinge between the historical recital closing at 135:12 and the idol polemic opening at 135:15: it neither continues the third-person recital's unbroken run nor opens the polemic's own topic.
rejected_alternative: Attaching this couplet to the preceding historical recital (135:5-12) was considered and rejected for the second-person vocative that opens 135:13; attaching it to the idol polemic that follows (135:15-18) was also considered and rejected because 135:14 names Yahweh's compassion on his own people, not yet the idols' impotence that 135:15 begins.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person vocative address to Yahweh ("Yahweh" named twice) opens web:Ps.135.13, unlike the third person on both sides of this span
no selah in Ps.135.13-Ps.135.14 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit is a typed relation to Ps 115's idol polemic: a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds 135:16 and 135:18 matching Ps 115's parallel verses letter-for-letter, while 135:15 opens with a different construct phrase and 135:17 compresses Ps 115's fuller list of inert body parts into a shorter clause. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring liturgical unit, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.
rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 135:14 instead, to fold in Yahweh's compassion as a foil to the idols' impotence, was considered; kept separate because 135:14 stays within the historical recital's third-person report of Yahweh's own acts, not yet the idols' inertness that 135:15 introduces as a fresh topic.
observed_substrate_signals: byte comparison (verse_map_oshb.json, this psalm's own text) against Ps 115's idol polemic: 135:16 and 135:18 match letter-for-letter; 135:15's opening differs; 135:17 is shorter than its Ps 115 counterpart -- a typed relation, not a merged row
no selah in Ps.135.15-Ps.135.18 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

rationale: A fourfold bless-call opens “בֵּ֣ית יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.19) -- “House of Israel, praise Yahweh! House of Aaron, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.19) -- and continues “בֵּ֣ית הַ֭לֵּוִי בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.20) -- “House of Levi, praise Yahweh! You who fear Yahweh, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.20). Four addressee groups are named across these two verses (house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, those who fear Yahweh); comparison against Ps 115's own bless-call (Israel, house of Aaron, fearers of Yahweh) and Ps 118's own call-and-response (the same three) finds both naming three groups where this psalm names four, adding house of Levi as a fourth member. The imperative vocative form returns after the idol polemic, bracketing the psalm with its opening call, and web:Ps.135.21's closing benediction carries this psalm's own verse-final hallelu-Yah, “Blessed be Yahweh from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. Praise Yah!”
rejected_alternative: Treating 135:19-20's fourfold call and 135:21's benediction as two rows was considered; kept together because 135:21 closes the same imperative sequence that 135:19-20 open, without introducing a fresh addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: bless-call names four addressee groups across web:Ps.135.19-Ps.135.20 (2 verses): house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, those who fear Yahweh
Ps 115 and Ps 118's own parallel calls name three groups (Israel, house of Aaron, fearers of Yahweh), without house of Levi
hallelu-Yah verse-final at web:Ps.135.21, closing the frame opened at 135:1 and 135:3 (psalm_device_inventory.json halleluyah.verse_final)

rationale: Untitled, Psalm 136 opens “הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב” (oshb:Ps.136.1) -- “Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good,” (web:Ps.136.1) -- the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH formula listed in psalm_device_inventory.json's hodu_openings (one of six book-wide, alongside 33:2, 105:1, 107:1, 118:1, 118:29). A triadic escalation follows: “Give thanks to the God of gods” (web:Ps.136.2), “Give thanks to the Lord of lords” (web:Ps.136.3), each closed by this psalm's own refrain. A verse-by-verse comparison of the refrain's own tail across all 26 verses of this psalm finds “כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.1) present in all 26, but not always in the same spelling: 136:3 spells the refrain's "forever" defectively, “לְעֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.3) (no vav in the second word), against the plene spelling in the other 25 -- an erratum-class spelling variant, not a break in the refrain's presence. web:Ps.136.4 then drops the imperative hodu-plus-object frame for a participial construction ("to him who…") that runs through the rest of the psalm, marking this row's own close.
rejected_alternative: Extending the row through 136:4 was considered, since 136:4's own participle still names an attribute of Yahweh; rejected because 136:1-3 share one grammatical frame (imperative hodu + direct object) that 136:4 replaces with a participial construction sustained through the rest of the psalm.
observed_substrate_signals: hodu-le-YHWH verse-initial at web:Ps.136.1 (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings)

sweep: 26 of 26 verses in Ps 136 carry the closing refrain tail (direct verse-by-verse comparison of the final three words of each verse's own oshb text); 25 spelled plene, 1 (oshb:Ps.136.3) spelled defectively -- both attested spellings swept
grammatical frame shifts from imperative-plus-object (136:1-3) to participial construction beginning web:Ps.136.4
device_notes: Psalm 136's rows share a single parent composition throughout.

rationale: “לְעֹשֵׂ֣ה הַ֭שָּׁמַיִם בִּתְבוּנָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.136.5) -- “to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his loving kindness endures forever;” (web:Ps.136.5) -- opens the creation recital, continuing through the great wonders of web:Ps.136.4, the earth spread above the waters (web:Ps.136.6), the great lights (web:Ps.136.7), and their assignment to rule day and night (web:Ps.136.8-9). Every verse (6 of 6, 136:4-9) keeps the participial "to him who…" construction and closes with this psalm's refrain. The row's content turns from cosmic creation to Israel's history at its own close, where web:Ps.136.10 turns to Egypt.
rejected_alternative: A seam within 136:4-9, separating the general "great wonders" of 136:4 from the specific creation acts of 136:5-9, was considered; rejected as no grammatical marker distinguishes 136:4 from what follows -- the whole span is one uninterrupted participial chain under the psalm's own refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: participial "to him who…" construction runs unbroken from web:Ps.136.4 through web:Ps.136.9; the Hebrew is one continuous syntactic chain across this book-wide seam (not a self-standing sentence break)
content turns from cosmic creation (136:4-9) to Egypt/exodus beginning web:Ps.136.10, without a grammatical-form change

rationale: The recital turns to the exodus: “to him who struck down the Egyptian firstborn,” (web:Ps.136.10), Israel brought out (web:Ps.136.11), with a strong hand and outstretched arm (web:Ps.136.12), the Red Sea divided (“לְגֹזֵ֣ר יַם ס֭וּף לִגְזָרִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.136.13)), Israel passed through (web:Ps.136.14), and Pharaoh's army overthrown in the sea (web:Ps.136.15). All 6 verses in this span (136:10-15) close with this psalm's refrain, as do all 26 verses of the book. The row's content turns from the sea crossing to the wilderness march at its own close, where web:Ps.136.16 turns to the wilderness.
rejected_alternative: Folding 136:10 into the preceding creation row (136:4-9) was considered, since both share the participial frame; rejected because 136:10 is the recital's opening Egypt-naming verse, opening the exodus content movement rather than closing the creation one.
observed_substrate_signals: content moves from Egypt's plague (136:10) through the Red Sea crossing (136:13-15); grammatical form (participle/finite-verb alternation) does not itself mark this row's edges -- content alone does
wilderness march named beginning at web:Ps.136.16, immediately after this row's own close

rationale: The recital moves from wilderness to conquest: Yahweh led his people through the wilderness (web:Ps.136.16), struck great kings (web:Ps.136.17) and killed mighty kings (web:Ps.136.18), naming them by name -- “לְ֭סִיחוֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ הָאֱמֹרִ֑י” (oshb:Ps.136.19) (web:Ps.136.19) and “וּ֭לְעוֹג מֶ֣לֶךְ הַבָּשָׁ֑ן” (oshb:Ps.136.20) (web:Ps.136.20) -- before their land is given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.136.21-22). This Sihon/Og notice is a typed relation to Ps 135's own Sihon/Og verse: byte comparison of both psalms' own text finds 136:19's naming of Sihon and 136:20's naming of Og matching Ps 135's phrasing word for word, while the land-grant clause that follows (136:21-22) varies from Ps 135's own wording in two words. web:Ps.136.23 then shifts from third-person "his people" to first-person-plural "us", marking this row's own close.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the wilderness march (136:16) from the conquest naming (136:17-22) was considered; rejected because no grammatical or addressee change divides them -- both stay third-person description of Yahweh's acts toward "his people"/"Israel" under the shared refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: byte comparison (verse_map_oshb.json) against Ps 135's own Sihon/Og notice: web:Ps.136.19-Ps.136.20's naming of Sihon and Og repeats Ps 135's phrasing word for word; the land-grant clause of 136:21-22 differs from Ps 135's wording in two words -- a typed relation, not a merged row
first-person-plural "us"/"our" opens immediately after this row's own close, at web:Ps.136.23

rationale: “שֶׁ֭בְּשִׁפְלֵנוּ זָ֣כַר לָ֑נוּ” (oshb:Ps.136.23) -- “who remembered us in our low estate,” (web:Ps.136.23) -- turns from the historical third person to first-person-plural address, continuing “and has delivered us from our adversaries,” (web:Ps.136.24) before web:Ps.136.25 widens to a universal, impersonal close, “who gives food to every creature,” before the psalm's own final verse returns to its opening imperative, “ה֭וֹדוּ לְאֵ֣ל הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם” (oshb:Ps.136.26) -- "Oh give thanks to the God of heaven," (web:Ps.136.26) -- an inclusio repeating web:Ps.136.1's own hodu-le-YHWH opening word for word. The row closes the psalm at its own closing verse.
rejected_alternative: Treating 136:26 as its own one-verse coda, separate from 136:23-25, was considered for its inclusio function; rejected as too short to divide from the closing movement it caps, and the psalm's own refrain still binds it to 136:23-25 without a fresh addressee change.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person-plural "us"/"our" opens web:Ps.136.23, against the third-person "him"/"his" of all 19 verses from 136:4 through 136:22
web:Ps.136.26's opening word repeats web:Ps.136.1's own opening word (byte comparison, verse_map_oshb.json), an inclusio closing the psalm

rationale: Untitled, Psalm 137 opens “עַ֥ל נַהֲר֨וֹת בָּבֶ֗ל שָׁ֣ם יָ֭שַׁבְנוּ” (oshb:Ps.137.1) -- “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.” (web:Ps.137.1) -- a first-person-plural scene of captivity, continuing “On the willows in that land, we hung up our harps.” (web:Ps.137.2), then reporting the captors' own demand in quotation, “Sing us one of the songs of Zion!” (web:Ps.137.3), before the exiles' own rhetorical refusal closes the row, “How can we sing Yahweh's song in a foreign land?” (web:Ps.137.4). All 4 verses of this span stay in the communal "we" voice; the row closes where that voice narrows to first-person-singular at web:Ps.137.5.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the captivity scene (137:1-2) from the captors' demand and the refusal (137:3-4) was considered; rejected because both share the same first-person-plural "we" voice with no addressee shift between them, and 137:4's question is the direct rhetorical answer to 137:3's own demand.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person-plural "we" voice runs unbroken from web:Ps.137.1 through web:Ps.137.4
quoted captors' demand at web:Ps.137.3 ("Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"), answered by the rhetorical question of web:Ps.137.4
no selah in Ps.137.1-Ps.137.4 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)
device_notes: A single parent, Psalm 137, holds all of this lament's rows together.

rationale: The voice narrows from communal "we" to first-person-singular self-imprecation: “אִֽם אֶשְׁכָּחֵ֥ךְ יְֽרוּשָׁלִָ֗ם” (oshb:Ps.137.5) -- “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.” (web:Ps.137.5) -- continuing “Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I don't remember you, if I don't prefer Jerusalem above my chief joy.” (web:Ps.137.6). Jerusalem is addressed directly by name in apostrophe across both verses, distinct from the preceding "we"-voiced captivity scene and the imprecation against Edom and Babylon that follows in second person address to Yahweh.
rejected_alternative: Folding this couplet into the following imprecation (137:7-9) was considered, since both continue the psalm's private voice; rejected because 137:5-6 is self-imprecation addressed to Jerusalem by apostrophe, while 137:7 opens a fresh imperative addressed to Yahweh against a third party.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person-singular "I"/"my" self-imprecation opens web:Ps.137.5, against the first-person-plural "we" of 137:1-4
Jerusalem addressed by name in direct apostrophe across web:Ps.137.5-Ps.137.6

rationale: The imprecation turn opens “זְכֹ֤ר יְהוָ֨ה לִבְנֵ֬י אֱד֗וֹם” (oshb:Ps.137.7) -- “Remember, Yahweh, against the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem,” (web:Ps.137.7) -- quoting Edom's own cry, “Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!” The address then turns from Yahweh to Babylon directly, “Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, he will be happy who repays you, as you have done to us.” (web:Ps.137.8), closing with the psalm's own harsh closing line, “Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.” (web:Ps.137.9). The row groups the Edom imprecation and the Babylon imprecation as one closing movement, opened by the second-person imperative to Yahweh at 137:7 and sustained in second-person address (now to Babylon) through the psalm's end.
rejected_alternative: Separating the Edom imprecation (137:7) from the Babylon imprecation (137:8-9) into two rows was considered, since the addressee shifts from Yahweh to Babylon between them; rejected because both remain second-person imperative/vocative address sustained without a first-person or third-person report intervening, and the row is already short.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person imperative address to Yahweh opens web:Ps.137.7, quoting Edom's own cry ("Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!")
addressee turns to "Daughter of Babylon" in direct second-person vocative at web:Ps.137.8, sustained through the psalm's close at 137.9
no selah in Ps.137.7-Ps.137.9 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

rationale: The composition opens with a thanksgiving vow, “I will give you thanks with my whole heart” (web:Ps.138.1), and closes with a confident petition, “Don’t forsake the works of your own hands” (web:Ps.138.8), an envelope from vow to petition that runs across only 8 verses -- within the short-psalm threshold for a whole-psalm row. The middle carries one continuous address: the kings’ report (web:Ps.138.4-5) and the affliction/deliverance turn (web:Ps.138.6-7) develop the opening vow rather than opening an independently marked strophe (no selah, no vocative reset, no genre-label shift inside the body).
rejected_alternative: Splitting after web:Ps.138.4’s shift from personal thanksgiving to the kings’ response was considered, but web:Ps.138.5 continues the same third-person report about Yahweh’s ways without a vocative reset strong enough to carry a strophe break in a psalm this short.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.138.1 opens with first-person thanksgiving vow addressed to Yahweh
web:Ps.138.8 closes with imperative petition, same addressee
no web_selah flag anywhere in Ps.138.1-8 (verse_map_web.json)
psalm length 8 verses sits at the owner-ruled whole-psalm threshold (§6)
device_notes: Each row here traces to the one Psalm-138 parent.

rationale: The meditation opens its known movement on the root pair “יְהוָ֥ה חֲ֝קַרְתַּ֗נִי וַתֵּדָֽע” (oshb:Ps.139.1) -- “Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me” (web:Ps.139.1) -- which surveys Yahweh’s knowledge of the psalmist’s sitting/rising, path, and unspoken word (web:Ps.139.2-4) before closing on the psalmist’s own confession, “This knowledge is beyond me” (web:Ps.139.6). The root pair recurs at web:Ps.139.23 (“Search me, God, and know my heart”), so this opening row anchors one half of the psalm’s inclusio.
rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.139.3’s summary of “all my ways” was considered, but vv4-6 continue the same second-person survey of Yahweh’s knowledge without a discourse-marking shift until the rhetorical questions of web:Ps.139.7.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.139.1 root pair יְהוָ֥ה חֲ֝קַרְתַּ֗נִי וַתֵּדָֽע (search/know, byte-spliced)
oshb:Ps.139.23 root pair חָקְרֵ֣נִי אֵ֭ל וְדַ֣ע (search/know, byte-spliced) -- shared roots with 139.1

device_notes: The strophes gather under Psalm 139 as one unit. — Psalm 139. Its four movements (known, present, formed, tested) share one inclusio frame.

rationale: The movement turns from Yahweh’s knowledge to Yahweh’s presence, opening with the rhetorical double question “Where could I go from your Spirit? Or where could I flee from your presence?” (web:Ps.139.7), surveying heaven, Sheol, and the wings of the dawn (web:Ps.139.8-10) before closing on darkness and light (web:Ps.139.11-12). An anaphoric “gam” (גם, “even/also”) opens both web:Ps.139.10 and web:Ps.139.12 at the consonantal (skeleton) tier, tying the unit's middle to its own close rather than to the prior movement's close at web:Ps.139.6.
rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at web:Ps.139.10 (after “your right hand will hold me”) was considered, but vv11-12 continue the same spatial-evasion logic under the rhetorical-question frame opened at web:Ps.139.7, so the movement is kept whole through its own close.

rationale: The movement shifts to the psalmist’s formation, opening “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb” (web:Ps.139.13), grounding the prior movements’ claims in a remembered event, and continuing through the “fearfully and wonderfully made” confession (web:Ps.139.14) and the divine book of ordained days (web:Ps.139.16) to close on “When I wake up, I am still with you” (web:Ps.139.18) -- a relational close distinct from the abrupt imprecation that opens web:Ps.139.19.

rationale: The closing movement turns abruptly to imprecation, “If only you, God, would kill the wicked” (web:Ps.139.19), against those who “take your name in vain” (web:Ps.139.20) and whom the psalmist hates “with perfect hatred” (web:Ps.139.22), before pivoting at “חָקְרֵ֣נִי אֵ֭ל וְדַ֣ע” (oshb:Ps.139.23) -- “Search me, God, and know my heart” -- which answers web:Ps.139.1’s opening root pair and closes the psalm’s own inclusio through web:Ps.139.24’s petition to be led “in the everlasting way.”
rejected_alternative: Splitting the imprecation (vv19-22) from the closing self-examination (vv23-24) into two strophes was considered, but web:Ps.139.23 directly answers web:Ps.139.1's opening root pair and closes the whole composition's frame, so the two halves are kept together as the unit that completes the psalm.

rationale: The title לְדָוִ֨ד (Hebrew: for David) sits as the prefix of MT verse 1 (web:Ps.144.0 = oshb:Ps.144.1), and the verse body opens the blessing formula, בָּ֘ר֤וּךְ יְהוָ֨ה צוּרִ֗י (oshb:Ps.144.1), “Blessed be Yahweh, my rock, who trains my hands to war, and my fingers to battle” (web:Ps.144.1), stacking an epithet chain in the next verse, חַסְדִּ֥י וּמְצוּדָתִי֮ מִשְׂגַּבִּ֪י וּֽמְפַלְטִ֫י (oshb:Ps.144.2), “my loving kindness, my fortress, my high tower, my deliverer” (web:Ps.144.2). The strophe turns to a rhetorical meditation without changing addressee, מָה אָ֭דָם (oshb:Ps.144.3), “Yahweh, what is man, that you care for him?” (web:Ps.144.3), resolved in the breath-and-shadow figure of “Man is like a breath. His days are like a shadow that passes away.” (web:Ps.144.4). It closes before the fresh imperative petition that opens web:Ps.144.5.

rationale: A fresh imperative petition opens the strophe, הַט שָׁמֶ֣יךָ וְתֵרֵ֑ד (oshb:Ps.144.5), “Part your heavens, Yahweh, and come down. Touch the mountains, and they will smoke.” (web:Ps.144.5), continuing through the lightning-and-arrows theophany of web:Ps.144.6 into the rescue plea, שְׁלַ֥ח יָדֶ֗יךָ מִמָּ֫ר֥וֹם פְּצֵ֣נִי וְ֭הַצִּילֵנִי (oshb:Ps.144.7), “Stretch out your hand from above, rescue me, and deliver me out of great waters, out of the hands of foreigners” (web:Ps.144.7), and closing on the foreigners' own falsehood, “whose mouths speak deceit, whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” (web:Ps.144.8). The parted-heavens, smoking-mountain, and scattered-lightning imagery echoes Ps 18's own storm theophany (web:Ps.18.9-web:Ps.18.14), and the many-waters rescue answers web:Ps.18.16's own many-waters line.
